en: The Teaching of Vimalakīrti;
homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Thus have I heard.
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vaiśālī in the Āmrapālī grove, together with a great saṅgha of eight thousand bhikṣus.
All were arhats whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had attained mastery, whose minds were well-liberated, whose wisdom was well-liberated,

who were noble thoroughbreds, great dragons, who had done what was to be done, accomplished their task, laid down the burden, attained their own goal, completely destroyed the fetters of existence, whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge, and who had reached the supreme perfection of mastery over all mental states.
And there were thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas, renowned for their supernormal knowledges, all of whom had emerged through the cultivation of great supernormal powers,
were sustained by the empowerment of the Buddha,
and served as guardians of the city of the True Dharma.
by those who uphold the true Dharma,
who utter the great lion's roar,
and whose voices resound throughout the ten directions;

They are spiritual friends who do not need to be requested by all sentient beings, those who ensure that the lineage of the Three Jewels is not interrupted, and those who have struck down Māra and his adversaries.
They were unconquerable by any proponents of opposing doctrines,
endowed with mindfulness, concentration, and dhāraṇīs,
and free from all hindrances and obsessions.
They were established in unobstructed liberation;
they possessed indestructible eloquence;
and they had emerged through generosity, self-control, restraint, discipline, ethical conduct, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, and skillful means.
They were endowed with the patient acceptance of the non-apprehension and non-arising of phenomena;
they set in motion the irreversible wheel of Dharma;
and they were sealed with the seal of the markless.
They were skilled in knowing the faculties of all sentient beings, they strode with the fearlessnesses that are unsurpassed by any assembly,
and they had accumulated a great store of merit and wisdom.
with bodies adorned with the primary and secondary marks, possessing supreme beauty,
yet devoid of ornaments;
They had risen up with fame and renown as lofty as the peak of Mount Meru;
they had attained an unbreakable faith in the Buddha-dharma through a firm resolve like a diamond;
and they were those who rained down the nectar-water from the scattering of the jewels of the Dharma.
With voices purified by the sounds of the vocal organs and the cries of all sentient beings;

having completely severed the continuity of the latent predispositions for views regarding the beginningless and endless [cycle of existence] through the realization of the profound Dharma of dependent origination;
and possessing a roar like that of a lion who is free from fear.
They had transcended both the similar and the dissimilar;

they were great caravan leaders who had fully realized the jewel of the Dharma through wisdom; they were skilled in all phenomena that are straight, subtle, gentle, difficult to see, and difficult to understand; and their range of knowledge had entered into the minds and intentions of sentient beings regarding their origins.

They had been consecrated by the empowerment of the peerless wisdom of a Buddha; they were established in the resolute intention toward the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the unique qualities of a Buddha; they had cast off the moats of all miserable states, evil destinies, and perditions;
and they manifested rebirth in the realms of existence through intentional resolve.
They were great kings of physicians, skilled in the methods for disciplining all sentient beings,
and devoted to the application of the medicinal remedies of the Dharma as was appropriate for each.
endowed with mines of infinite virtues,
adorned with the magnificent arrays of qualities of infinite buddha-fields,
and whose hearing and sight are never in vain;
With unfailing strides,
they possess boundless floods of virtues that have been proclaimed through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons.
For example, there was the bodhisattva mahāsattva named Samadarśin, and the one named Samaviṣamadarśin.
and by Samādhivikurvaṇarāja, Dharmeśvara, and Dharmaketu;
and Prabhāketu, and Prabhāvyūha, and Mahāvyūha,
and Ratnakūṭa, and Pratibhānakūṭa,
and Ratnamudrāhasta;
with hands constantly raised,
with hands always forming the utpala gesture,
and with constant longing;
and with Nityaprahasitapramuditendriya, Prāmodyarāja,
and Devarāja;
and by Praṇidhiprayātaprāpta, and by Pratisaṃvitpraṇādaprāpta,
and by Gaganagañja;
and Ratnolkādhārin, and Ratnavīra, and Ratnaśrī;
and Ratnanandin, and Indrajālin, and Jālinīprabha;
and by Anāraṃbaṇadhyāyin,
and by Prajñākūṭa, and by Ratnajaḥ;
and by Mārapramardin, and by Vidyuddeva, and by Vikurvaṇarāja;
And by Lakṣaṇakūṭa,
and by Lakṣaṇakūṭasamatikrānta,
and by Siṃhaghoṣābhigarjitasvara.
And by Śailaśikharasaṃghaṭṭanarāja, and by Gandhahastin,
and by Gajagandhahastin;
and Satatodyukta, and Anikṣiptadhura,
and Sumati;
and Sujāta, and Padmaśrīgarbha, and Padmavyūha;
and by Avalokiteśvara,
Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Brahmajālin;
and Ratnayaṣṭi, and Mārajit, and Kṣetrālaṃkṛta,
And with Maṇiratnacchatra,
Suvarṇacūḍa, and Maṇicūḍa;
And with Maitreya, and the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta,
and thirty-two thousand Bodhisattvas headed by these;
And ten thousand Brahmās, headed by Jaṭibrahmā,
having come from many world-systems of four great continents to behold, pay homage to, attend upon, and hear the Dharma from the Blessed One,
had assembled right there in that assembly.

Twelve thousand Śakras, having arrived from other four-continent world systems, were assembled right there in that assembly. Likewise, others of great renown— Śakras, Brahmās, World-protectors, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas— were also assembled and seated right there in that assembly.
Likewise, the fourfold assembly—monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen—had gathered there.

Seated upon the Lion Throne in the Śrīgarbha (Womb of Glory), the Blessed One, surrounded and honored by an assembly of many hundreds of thousands, was teaching the Dharma. Like Sumeru, the king of mountains, rising up from the midst of the ocean, he outshone the entire assembly, shining, glowing, and radiating splendor.
Then the Licchavi youth Ratnākara, together with about five hundred Licchavi youths,
took up parasols made of the seven precious gems and departed from the great city of Vaiśālī, proceeding toward the Āmrapālī grove where the Blessed One was staying.

Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One seven times, and covered the Blessed One with those parasols as they had been brought; having so covered him,
he stood to one side.
As soon as those jeweled parasols were released, by the power of the Buddha, they immediately became a single great jeweled parasol.
And by that great jeweled parasol, this entire trichiliocosm was seen to be completely covered;
indeed, whatever the extent and breadth of this trichiliocosm, it was all encompassed by it.
He was seen within that great jewel parasol;

and whatever Sumerus there are in this trichiliocosm— the kings of great mountains, such as the Himavat, Mucilinda, Mahāmucilinda, Gandhamādana, and the jewel mountains, as well as the Cakravāḍas and Mahācakravāḍas— all of them were likewise seen within that single great jewel parasol.
Whatever great oceans, lakes, ponds, rivers, or small streams flow here in this trichiliocosm,
all of them were seen within that single great jewel parasol.
Likewise, whatever celestial palaces of the sun and moon and the forms of the stars exist here in this trichiliocosm [were also seen there].
Whether they were the abodes of gods, or the abodes of nāgas, or the abodes of yakṣas, or the abodes of gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas,
or the abodes of the four great kings, or villages, cities, towns, provinces, and royal capitals—
all of these were likewise seen within that single great jewel parasol.
Furthermore, whatever Dharma-teaching of the Blessed Buddhas proceeds throughout the worlds of the ten directions,
that too was heard as issuing forth from that very single great jewel parasol.
Thereupon, the entire assembly was struck with wonder at having witnessed such a great miracle from the presence of the Blessed One.
Having seen [this], she was satisfied, uplifted, and joyful; filled with gladness and happiness, she stood bowing to the Tathāgata, gazing at him without blinking.

Then, indeed, the Licchavi youth Ratnākara, having witnessed such a great miracle from the presence of the Blessed One, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, and [turned] toward where...
Having bowed with palms joined toward the Blessed One, he praised the Blessed One with verses:
"O you whose eyes are as broad as the petals of a beautiful, pure, and excellent lotus; O you of pure intention who have reached the pinnacle of the perfection of tranquility (*śamatha*);
O you who have accumulated a store of auspicious karma and possess immeasurable, vast qualities—I bow to you, O Śramaṇa, the guide upon the path of peace. (1)
Behold the supernatural power of the Leader, the Bull among Men! The excellent illumination of the Sugata’s field is clearly visible;
and that sublime discourse on the Dharma, leading to the deathless, is heard from the expanse of the sky in its entirety. // 2 //
By means of Dharma, you have conquered this excellent kingdom of Dharma; O Conqueror of Enemies, you bestow both Dharma and wealth upon the world.
Skilled in the distinctions of Dharma, seer of the ultimate truth, Lord of Dharma—I bow my head to you, the King of Dharma. //3//
You speak words that are neither existent nor non-existent; all these phenomena arise in dependence upon causes.
Herein there is no self, no agent, and no experiencer; yet not even the slightest virtuous or non-virtuous action perishes. // 4 //

O Lord of Munis, Māra has been conquered by you along with his army; you have attained the auspicious, immortal, peaceful, supreme, and foremost awakening, in which the movements of mind and thought are no longer perceived, and into which the hosts of all false teachers cannot penetrate. (5)
And you have set in motion the wheel, which has three turnings and many aspects, which brings peace and is pure by nature;
O King of Dharma, a marvel to gods and men, you have manifested the Three Jewels there at that time. (6)
Those who have been correctly disciplined by you through the jewel of the Dharma are free from conceptual construction and are perpetually serene;
I bow my head to that supreme physician, the immeasurable ocean of virtues, who brings an end to birth, old age, and death. (7)
Honored with hospitality, you do not become conceited; like Mount Meru, you maintain equal compassion toward those of immoral conduct and those of virtuous conduct.
O jewel among beings, whose mind is as luminous as space and who dwells in equanimity—who indeed would not offer worship to you? (8)
O Great Sage, these gathered people gaze upon your face with serene minds;
and all behold the Jina before them, the unique mark of a Buddha belonging to the Jina. (9)

The Blessed One utters but a single sound, yet the assembly understands it in various ways; each person perceives its meaning according to their own capacity—this is the unique quality of a Buddha belonging to the Victor. (10)
When a single word is uttered, you cause some to dwell [in faith] while others turn away in disillusionment;
you pacify the doubts of those who seek them—this is the unique characteristic of a Buddha, O Leader. // 11 //
I pay homage to you, O One of Ten Powers, whose valor is truth; I pay homage to you who have attained fearlessness and are self-confident.
I pay homage to you who have reached certainty in the unique qualities of a Buddha; I pay homage to you, the leader of the entire world. 12.

I pay homage to you who have severed the bonds of the fetters; I pay homage to you who have gone to the further shore and stand upon dry land. I pay homage to the deliverer of suffering beings; I pay homage to you who are independent within the course of saṃsāra. // 13 //

O Lotus-like Sage, you have attained composure among beings; though you traverse all states of existence, your mind is liberated from them. Like a lotus in the water, you are unsullied, for you have cultivated emptiness. 14.
All signs have been thoroughly eliminated in every way, and no aspiration toward anything exists for you.
I pay homage to the inconceivable, great majesty of the Buddha, which is like space and free from dependence. 15.
Then the Licchavi youth Ratnākara, having praised the Blessed One with these verses, addressed the Blessed One as follows:
“Blessed One, these five hundred Licchavi youths have all set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
They are asking about the purification of the buddha-field: ‘What is the purification of the buddha-field for bodhisattvas?’”
"Therefore, O Blessed One, may the Tathāgata please teach the purification of the buddha-fields for these bodhisattvas.
When this had been said, the Blessed One gave his approval to the Licchavi youth Ratnākara: "Excellent, excellent, young man!"
Excellent indeed, O youth, that you inquire of the Tathāgata concerning the purification of the Buddha-field.
Therefore, youth, listen well and attend closely;
I shall speak to you regarding the purification of the Buddha-fields of the Bodhisattvas.
"Excellent, Blessed One! Ratnākara, the Licchavi youth, and those five hundred Licchavi youths replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to them:
"Noble son, the field of sentient beings is the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva."
For what reason?
To whatever extent a bodhisattva brings about the accumulation of merit for sentient beings, to that same extent he takes hold of a buddhafield;
in whatever manner the discipline of sentient beings occurs, in that very manner he takes hold of a buddhafield.
He takes hold of such a buddha-field by means of which entry into a buddha-field sentient beings enter into the wisdom of a Buddha;
he takes hold of such a buddha-field by means of which entry into a buddha-field the noble forms of the faculties arise in sentient beings.
For what reason?
"Noble son, the buddha-field of bodhisattvas is produced from the welfare of sentient beings.
Ratnākara, it is just as if one wished to construct space in whatever way one desired; one might construct it accordingly, yet space cannot be constructed, nor can it be adorned."
In the same way, Ratnākara, having realized that all phenomena are equal to space,
a bodhisattva constructs a buddha-field exactly as he wishes to construct it for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
yet the spatial nature of the buddha-field cannot be constructed, nor can it be adorned.
Furthermore, Ratnākara,
the field of intention is a bodhisattva’s buddha-field;
when he has attained awakening, beings who are free from deceit and guile are reborn in his buddha-field.
Noble son, the field of resolute intention is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, sentient beings who have accumulated all the provisions of merit arise in his buddha-field.
The field of application is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva.
When he has attained awakening, those beings who are established in all wholesome qualities are reborn in that buddhafield.
The bodhisattva’s noble production of the thought of awakening is his buddhafield;
when he has attained awakening, those beings who have set out in the Mahāyāna arise in that buddhafield.
The field of generosity is the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, all beings who have practiced total renunciation are born in that Buddha-field.
The field of ethical discipline is the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva.
When he has attained awakening, beings who are fulfilled in all their aspirations and who preserve the ten paths of wholesome action will be born in that buddha-field.
Noble son, the field of patience is a bodhisattva’s buddha-field;
when he has attained awakening, beings adorned with the thirty-two marks, who have reached the perfections of patience, self-control, and tranquility, will be born in his buddha-field.
The field of vigor is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, beings who have initiated vigor in the pursuit of all wholesome qualities are born in his buddha-field.
The field of meditative concentration is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva.
When he has attained awakening, beings who are concentrated through mindfulness and clear comprehension are born in his buddha-field.
The field of wisdom is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field;
when he has attained awakening, beings who are fixed in rightness are born in his buddha-field.
The four immeasurables are the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, beings who dwell in loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are born in his Buddha-field.
Noble son, the four means of attraction are the Buddha-field of a bodhisattva.
When he has attained awakening, beings who are comprised within all forms of liberation are born in his buddha-field.
Skill in means is the bodhisattva’s buddha-field;
when he has attained awakening, beings who are skilled in the investigation of all means are born in his buddha-field.
The thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (*bodhipakṣadharma*) are the buddha-field of a bodhisattva;

when he has attained awakening, those beings who know the methods of the right applications of mindfulness, the right abandonments, the bases of miraculous power, the faculties, the powers, the limbs of awakening, and the path arise in his buddha-field.
The mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanācitta*) is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva.
When he has attained awakening, his buddha-field is seen as adorned with all virtues.
Noble son, the teaching that pacifies the eight unfavorable conditions is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, there arises for him a buddha-field in which all states of woe are eradicated and the eight unfavorable conditions have been removed.
Abiding oneself in the precepts and not inciting others to transgressions is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva;
when he has attained awakening, even the word "transgression" does not exist in his buddha-field.
Purification of the ten paths of wholesome action, son of good family, is the buddha-field of a bodhisattva.

When he has attained awakening, beings will be born in his buddha-field who have a fixed lifespan, possess great wealth, live a life of celibacy, whose speech is adorned by words that accord with truth, who speak sweetly, whose assemblies are not divided, who are skilled at reconciling those who are divided, who are free from envy, whose minds are without malice, and who are endowed with right view.
Thus, noble son,
as many as are the applications of a bodhisattva, so many are his intentions; as many as are his intentions, so many are his resolute intentions.
As many as there are resolute intentions, so many are there profound contemplations; as many as there are profound contemplations, so many are there practices;
as many as there are practices, so many are there dedications.
As many as there are dedications, so many are the skillful means; as many as there are skillful means, so many are the purifications of the field;
and as is the purification of the field, so is the purification of sentient beings.

To whatever extent there is purity of sentient beings, to that same extent there is purity of knowledge; to whatever extent there is purity of knowledge, to that same extent there is purity of teaching;
to whatever extent there is purity of teaching, to that same extent there is purity of the practice of knowledge.
To whatever extent there is purity in the realization of knowledge, to that same extent there is purity of one’s own mind.
Therefore, noble son, a bodhisattva who wishes to purify a buddha-field should apply effort toward the purification of his own mind. Why is that?
To whatever extent there is purity of mind in a bodhisattva, to that same extent the purification of a buddha-field occurs.
Then, through the power of the Buddha, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:
"If, to whatever extent there is purity of mind, to that same extent the purification of a bodhisattva’s buddha-field occurs,"
"Let it not be that the mind of the Blessed One Śākyamuni was impure while he was practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva, such that this buddha-field appears so impure.
Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra with his own mind, said to the venerable Śāriputra:
"What do you think?"
"Śāriputra, do not say that the sun and moon are impure because one born blind does not see them.
He replied, "Certainly not, Blessed One; this is the fault of the one born blind, not of the sun and moon.

The Buddha said, "In the same way, Śāriputra, it is the fault of the ignorance of sentient beings that some beings do not perceive the magnificent array of the qualities and ornaments of the Tathāgata’s buddha-field."
"It is not the fault of the Tathāgata in this regard.
For, Śāriputra, the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata is perfectly pure; it is you who do not see it as such. Then the Brahmā Jaṭī said this to the elder Śāriputra:
Venerable Śāriputra, do not say that this buddha-field of the Tathāgata is impure;
for, Venerable Śāriputra, the buddha-field of the Blessed One is utterly pure,
just like the magnificent palaces of the Vaśavartin gods.
"O Blessed One, we see such magnificent arrays of qualities in the Buddha-field of the Blessed Śākyamuni.
Then the Elder Śāriputra said this to the Brahmā Jaṭin:
"But we, O Brahmā, see this great earth as uneven, with highs and lows, filled with thorns, precipices, mountain peaks, chasms, excrement, and cesspools."
The matted-hair ascetic Brahmā said:
"Surely, Venerable Śāriputra, your mind is uneven and your aspiration for the Buddha's wisdom is unpurified, since you perceive the Buddha-field in such a way.

However, Venerable Śāriputra, those bodhisattvas who possess a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings and whose aspiration for the Buddha's wisdom is purified—they perceive this Buddha-field as pure."
Then the Blessed One struck this great trichiliocosm with his big toe.
At that moment, this great trichiliocosm became composed of and adorned with hundreds of thousands of various jewels;
it appeared just like the world-system of the Tathāgata Ratnavyūha, which is arrayed with the infinite jewel-ornaments of virtue. Such was the appearance of this world-system.
There, that entire assembly was struck with wonder, perceiving themselves seated upon jewel lotuses.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, do you see these magnificent arrays of qualities of the buddha-field?"
He said: "I see them, Blessed One; these arrays, never before seen or heard, are now visible.
The Buddha said: "Śāriputra, my buddha-field is always like this.
However, for the sake of maturing inferior beings, the Tathāgata displays his buddha-field as being thus defiled by many faults."
"Śāriputra, it is just as when sons of the gods eat from a single vessel, yet according to the distinction of their respective accumulations of merit, the divine food *sudhā* appears before them;
even so, Śāriputra, beings born in a single Buddha-field perceive the magnificent arrays of qualities of the Buddhas' fields according to the purity of their own minds.

Furthermore, while this display of the magnificent array of ornaments of the Buddha-field was being shown, the minds of eighty-four thousand living beings were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment."
And those five hundred Licchavi youths who had come together with the Licchavi youth Ratnākara also attained the patient acceptance that accords with reality (*anulomikī kṣāntiḥ*).
Then the Blessed One withdrew that miraculous power once again;
thereupon, this buddha-field returned to its original nature.

There, among the gods and humans belonging to the vehicle of the śrāvakas, having realized, "Alas, all these conditioned phenomena are impermanent," the dustless and stainless Dharma-eye regarding phenomena was purified for thirty-two thousand living beings;
and the minds of eight thousand bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through non-clinging.

And for eighty-four thousand living beings who were devoted to the sublime Buddha-dharma— having realized that all phenomena are characterized by being manifestations and mere appearances— minds set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment arose.
The First Chapter: The Introduction to the Purification of the Buddha-field.
Now at that time, there lived in the great city of Vaiśālī a Licchavi named Vimalakīrti,
who had performed services for previous Victors and had planted roots of merit.
He has attended upon many Buddhas, has attained patient acceptance,
and has acquired eloquence.
He sported with the great superknowledges,
had attained the dhāraṇīs,
and had reached the grounds of self-confidence.
Having vanquished the adversaries that are the Māras,
he has deeply entered the profound method of the Dharma and is born from the perfection of wisdom.
He has reached the mastery of skillful means,
is endowed with eloquence,
and is skilled in the inclinations and conducts of sentient beings.
He has emerged through the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings;
he teaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate for each;
and he has reached certainty and exerted himself in this Mahāyāna.
One who performs actions after thorough examination,
established in the modes of conduct of a Buddha,
and entered into the ocean-like, supreme wisdom of a Buddha.
Praised, extolled, and lauded by all the Buddhas,
and honored by all the Śakras, Brahmās, and World-Protectors,
he dwelt in the great city of Vaiśālī through his skill in means for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
He possesses inexhaustible wealth for the sake of gathering in beings who are poor and destitute;
he maintains pure ethical discipline for the sake of gathering in those of immoral conduct;
and he has attained patience and self-control for the sake of gathering in those beings whose minds are wicked, malicious, resentful, and angry.
Possessing refined vigor for the sake of gathering in indolent beings;
established in meditative concentration, mindfulness, and samādhi for the sake of gathering in beings with distracted minds;
having attained certainty through wisdom for the sake of gathering in beings of poor wisdom.
Wearing white garments, he is perfected in the deportment of a śramaṇa;
though dwelling in a household, he is untainted by the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm;
yet he manifests a wife, sons, and daughters.
He is always a celibate practitioner,
surrounded by a retinue, and always dwells in solitude.
He is seen adorned with ornaments,
yet always distinguished by the [thirty-two] marks;
he is seen subsisting on food, drink, and nourishment.
He always subsists on the nourishment of meditative concentration;
he is seen in all gambling halls,
and he brings to maturity those beings whose minds are attached to the play of gambling.
Always practicing with heedfulness,
accepting all religious sects,
and possessing an unbreakable resolve toward the Buddha.
He is knowledgeable in the rules of all mundane and supramundane treatises,
always delights in the pleasure of the garden of Dharma,
and yet appears among all social gatherings.
He is honored as the foremost everywhere;
he speaks the Dharma and acts as a companion to the old, the middle-aged, and the young in order to conform to the world;
he is engaged in all worldly affairs, yet has no desire for gain or enjoyment.
He is seen at all crossroads and junctions for the sake of disciplining all sentient beings;
he enters into royal affairs for the sake of protecting sentient beings;
and he is seen in all assemblies for hearing the Dharma and in discourses for the purpose of turning others away from the Lesser Vehicle and establishing them in the Mahāyāna.
He frequents all writing schools in order to bring children to maturity; he enters all the households of courtesans in order to demonstrate the faults of sensual desire;
and he enters all the houses of musicians in order to establish mindfulness and clear comprehension.
Among merchants, he was honored as a merchant chief in order to proclaim the supreme Dharma;
among householders, he was honored as a householder in order to sever all grasping and clinging;
and among kṣatriyas, he was honored as a kṣatriya in order to establish them in the power of patience and gentleness.
Among the brahmins, he was esteemed as a brahmin for the purpose of destroying pride, intoxication, and arrogance;
among the ministers, he was esteemed as a minister for the purpose of engaging them in all royal affairs according to the Dharma;
and among the princes, he was esteemed as a prince for the purpose of turning them away from their longing for royal pleasures and power.
In the inner palaces, he is esteemed as a chamberlain for the sake of maturing women and young maidens;
he conforms to ordinary people in order to provide them with a focus on both common and distinguished merits;
and among the Śakras, he is esteemed as a Śakra for the sake of demonstrating the impermanence of sovereignty.
Among the Brahmās, he was honored as a Brahmā for the sake of manifesting special knowledge;
among the world-protectors, he was honored as a world-protector for the sake of protecting all sentient beings.
Thus, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti dwelt in the great city of Vaiśālī, endowed with such immeasurable skill in means and wisdom.
By means of skillful means, he manifested himself as being ill. While he was thus ill,

many thousands of beings— including kings, royal ministers, high officials, princes, courtiers, brahmins, householders, guild-leaders, merchants, and countryfolk from the great city of Vaiśālī, as well as others— approached him to inquire about his illness.
When they had approached him, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti,
taking this very body composed of the four great elements as his starting point, taught the Dharma:
"Friends, this body is thus impermanent."
Thus it is unstable, thus it is unreliable, thus it is weak.
Thus it is without essence;
thus it is decayed; thus it is transient.
Thus it is suffering, thus it is afflictive, thus it is subject to change.
In this way, friends, this body is a vessel for many diseases;
therein, a wise person should not place reliance.
Friends, this body is like a mass of foam, incapable of withstanding being rubbed.
This body is like a bubble, not remaining for long; this body is like a mirage, produced by the thirst of the afflictions;
this body is like the trunk of a plantain tree, because it lacks any core substance.
Alas, this body is like a machine, bound together by bones and sinews;
this body is like an illusion, produced by perversion;
this body is like a dream, a false appearance.
This body is like a reflection, appearing as a manifestation of prior karma;
this body is like an echo, because it is dependent upon conditions;
this body is like a cloud, characterized by the disappearance of mental turbulence.
This body is like lightning; it is subject to momentary disintegration and is unstable.
This body is without a master, having arisen from various conditions.
This body is devoid of agency, being like the earth.
This body is selfless, like water;
this body is soulless, like fire;
this body is devoid of a person, like wind.
This body is without intrinsic nature, resembling space.
This body is unproduced, a mere repository for the great elements.
This body is empty, devoid of a self or anything belonging to a self.
This body is insentient, resembling grass, wood, a wall, a clod of earth, or a reflection;
this body is motionless, functioning only through its connection to the mechanism of the winds;
this body is empty, a mere accumulation of impurities and putrefaction.

"Friends, the body of the Tathāgata is produced from immeasurable wholesome karma; you should therefore conceive a longing for it.

It is devoid of a life-principle, free from birth and death; it is without a person, severed from the prior and subsequent limits;

Detachment has no objective support as its destination; it is beyond syllables, the cessation of all speech, beyond utterance, and free from all waves of conceptualization.
It is omnipresent, resembling and equal to space; it is without color, mark, or shape, and is free from all activity;
it is without "mine" and free from the notion of possession.
Non-manifestation is free from mind, thought, and consciousness;
it is incomparable because it lacks any counterpart;
it is distinct from causes and non-superimposed upon conditions.
He is one who has entered into the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), who is concentrated in all phenomena,

and who is established in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) because of being utterly immovable.
It is immovable because it does not depend on the six sense objects; it has no coming or going anywhere because it is non-abiding;

Free from conjecture and exclusion, without addition or subtraction, and devoid of arising and ceasing.

You have entered into the convergence of the eight inopportune states, yet you have not attained [the marks of] physical characteristics; you are equal to affliction, yet you have realized purification; and that which is the absence of conflict (*araṇā*) for all sentient beings is also the absence of conflict for you, Venerable Sir.

you cause those who give alms-food to the Venerable One to fall into ruin;

for the Śrāvaka vehicle is painful."
"My disciples appear to me like those born blind regarding the knowledge of the diverse faculties of sentient beings.

And there was a need for milk;
so I stood at the gate of a certain wealthy brahmin’s house holding my bowl.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti arrived at that place.
Having paid homage to me, he said this:
"Venerable Ānanda, why do you stand here near the door of this house so early in the morning, carrying your bowl?
To him, I replied as follows:
"Householder, the Blessed One has a certain ailment in his body;
he requires milk for it, so I am searching for some."
He said this to me:
"Enough, Venerable Ānanda; do not speak thus.
For the body of the Tathāgata, Venerable Ānanda, has a vajra-like compactness; it has abandoned all unwholesome latencies and is endowed with all highly powerful wholesome dharmas."
"How could he have illness? How could he have affliction?
Venerable Ānanda, remain silent and go;
do not misrepresent the Blessed One."
Do not speak thus to anyone again,

lest the sons of the gods of great power and the bodhisattvas gathered from other buddha-fields hear you. Venerable Ānanda, even for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*), who possesses only meager roots of merit, no disease exists.
How could that Blessed One, who is endowed with immeasurable skillful means, have any illness?
Such a thing is impossible.
Go, go, Venerable Ānanda!
Do not cause me embarrassment;
let not the other sectarians, the Carakas, the Parivrājakas, the Nirgranthas, and the Ājīvakas hear this, lest it should occur to them thus: [“He is a liar”].
"Alas, what kind of teacher is this for them, who is not even able to protect himself when he is ill; how then will he be the protector of sentient beings who are ill?
Therefore, Reverend Ānanda, go quickly and in secret."
Let no one hear this!
But rather, Reverend Ānanda, the Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body, not a body of material things;
the Tathāgatas are the supramundane body, having transcended all worldly phenomena.
The body of the Tathāgata is free from affliction, being entirely liberated from all outflows;
the body of the Tathāgata is unconditioned, being beyond all enumeration.
For you, O Venerable One, to desire that he have illness is improper and inconsistent.
"Lord, a great sense of shame arose within me, thinking:
'May I not have misheard or wrongly grasped anything from the presence of the Blessed One.
Then I heard a voice from the sky:"
"It is just as the householder has explained, Ānanda.
Furthermore, since the Blessed One has appeared in this age of five corruptions, beings must be guided by means of a life of purposeful austerity and poverty."
"Therefore, Ānanda, go and take some milk; do not be ashamed.
"Lord, such are the instructions given by the Licchavi Vimalakīrti in his explanations and answers to questions."
"Therefore, Blessed One, I am not able to go to that son of good family to inquire after his illness.
In this way, those five hundred disciples, being unable to venture, informed the Blessed One;
and they reported to the Blessed One all the conversations they had held with the Licchavi Vimalakīrti.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Go, Maitreya, to inquire after the illness of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti. Maitreya replied:
“Blessed One, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire about his illness.
Why is that?
Blessed One, I recall:”

At one time, while I was engaged in a discourse on the Dharma with the divine son Saṃtuṣita and the other divine sons of the Tuṣita realm— concerning the irreversible stage of the bodhisattva mahāsattvas—
the Licchavi Vimalakīrti approached that place.
He said this to me:
"Maitreya, you have been prophesied by the Blessed One as being bound to only one more birth before attaining unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Maitreya, in which birth were you so prophesied?"
Is it by means of the past, the future, or the present?
In that regard, whatever birth was past has perished; whatever is yet to come has not yet arrived.
There is no duration for that which has arisen in the present,
as the Blessed One said: "For thus, O monk, moment by moment you are born, you age, you die, you pass away, and you are reborn."
And the entry into the fixed course of determination occurs through non-arising;
yet non-arising is not prophesied, nor is non-arising fully awakened to.
Maitreya, how then have you been prophesied by means of the arising of suchness or the cessation of suchness?
For suchness neither arises nor ceases,
and it will not cease.
That which is the suchness of all sentient beings and that which is the suchness of all phenomena is itself the suchness of Maitreya as well.
In this way, if you are prophesied, then all sentient beings are also prophesied.
Why is that?
Because suchness is not characterized by duality, nor is it characterized by diversity.
Therefore, when Maitreya awakens to supreme enlightenment, all sentient beings will also, at that very time, awaken to such an enlightenment.
For what reason?
For awakening is indeed the awakening to all sentient beings;
and when Maitreya enters final nirvana, all sentient beings will likewise enter final nirvana.
For what reason?
Because Tathāgatas do not enter parinirvāṇa as long as all sentient beings have not entered parinirvāṇa;
they perceive those sentient beings as being already parinirvāṇized by nature.
Therefore, Maitreya, do not deceive these sons of the gods here; do not mislead them.
No one at all is established in awakening, nor does anyone turn back from it.
Moreover, Maitreya, you should abandon this view of these sons of the gods which conceptualizes awakening;
for awakening is not fully realized by means of the body, nor by means of the mind.
Awakening is the complete stilling of all signs.
Enlightenment is the non-superimposition upon all objects;
enlightenment is the non-activity of all mental engagements;
enlightenment is the complete cutting off of all views.
Awakening is the departure from all conceptual constructions;
awakening is the dissociation from all agitation, conceit, and mental fluctuations;
awakening is the absence of basis for all vows.
Awakening is an unattached entry, free from all grasping; awakening abides in the station of the realm of phenomena;
awakening conforms to suchness.
Awakening is established in the limit of reality;
awakening is non-dual, being free from mind and phenomena;
awakening is equal, through its equality with space.
Enlightenment is unconditioned, being free from arising, ceasing, and alteration;
enlightenment is thorough knowledge of the mental activities and intentions of all sentient beings;
enlightenment is gateless with respect to the sense bases.
Awakening is unadulterated, being free from all afflictions along with their underlying tendencies and connections;
awakening does not abide in a location nor in a specific place, as it is free from both staying and not staying; awakening is established in suchness and is invisible from every side.
Awakening is a mere name, and that name is devoid of activity;
awakening is selfless, free from accumulation and rejection,
undisturbed, and pure by nature.
Awakening is luminous, being pure by nature; awakening is without grasping, being free from objective reference;
awakening is without diversity, because it is the realization of the equality of all phenomena.
Awakening is incomparable, being free from the presentation of analogies;
awakening is subtle, because it is difficult to realize;
awakening is omnipresent, because its intrinsic nature is like space.
She cannot be fully awakened to by means of body, speech,

or mind. Lord, while this teaching was being expounded here, two hundred sons of the gods from that assembly attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
and I became speechless.
"Therefore, Blessed One, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire about his illness.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Licchavi youth Prabhāvyūha: "Go, noble son, as an inquirer after the illness of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti."
Prabhāvyūha also said:
"Lord, I am not able to go as an inquirer after the illness of that good man.
For what reason? Because—"
I remember, Blessed One,
that on one occasion I was departing from the great city of Vaiśālī when the Licchavi Vimalakīrti was entering it.
Having saluted him, I said this to him:
"From where do you come, householder?
He spoke to me thus:
"I am coming from the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).
To him I said this:
"As for 'the seat of awakening,' whose name is that?"
He said this to me:
"Noble son, the 'seat of awakening' (bodhimaṇḍa) is the seat of intention, because it is uncontrived; it is the seat of application, because it brings undertakings to completion."
This is the essence of high resolve, because it is the attainment of distinction;
this is the essence of the thought of awakening, because it is free from forgetfulness;
this is the essence of giving, because it does not expect a karmic reward.
This is the essence of ethical discipline because it fulfills one's vows;
this is the essence of patience because the mind is unimpeded toward all sentient beings;
this is the essence of vigor because it is irreversible.
This is the essence of meditative concentration, through the adaptability of the mind;
this is the essence of wisdom, through direct perception;
this is the essence of loving-kindness, through equanimity toward all sentient beings.
This is the essence of compassion because of its endurance of weariness;
this is the essence of sympathetic joy because of its delight in the pleasure of the garden of Dharma;
this is the essence of equanimity because of its abandonment of both attachment and aversion.
This is the essence of supernormal knowledges because of the possession of the six supernormal knowledges; this is the essence of liberations because of the absence of conceptual construction;
this is the essence of skillful means because of the ripening of sentient beings.
This is the essence of the means of attraction, because it gathers all sentient beings;
this is the essence of learning, because its core is practice; this is the essence of profound reflection, because it consists of thorough investigation.
This is the maṇḍala of the factors conducive to awakening, because of the relinquishing of both the conditioned and the unconditioned;

this is the maṇḍala of truth, because of not deceiving the entire world; this is the maṇḍala of dependent origination, because of the exhaustion of the outflows of ignorance up to the exhaustion of the outflows of old age and death.
This is the essence that pacifies all afflictions, because it is the realization of things as they truly are;
this is the essence of all sentient beings, because sentient beings lack intrinsic nature;
this is the essence of all phenomena, because it is the realization of emptiness.

This is the essence that destroys all Māras, because it is immovable; this is the essence of the triple world, because it is free from setting out; this is the essence of the vigor of roaring the lion’s roar, because it is fearless and undaunted.

This is the maṇḍala of the powers, the fearlessnesses, and all the unique qualities of a Buddha, because it is entirely beyond reproach; this is the maṇḍala of the three types of knowledge, because of the complete exhaustion of the afflictions;
this is the maṇḍala of the realization of all phenomena in their entirety within a single moment of mind, because it is the full attainment of the wisdom of omniscience.

Thus, noble son, as many Bodhisattvas as there may be who lift and set down their feet in connection with the perfections, in connection with the maturation of sentient beings, in connection with the upholding of the true Dharma, and in connection with roots of merit—
all of them come from the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa).

They come from the Buddha-dharmas and they are established in the Buddha-dharmas. Lord, while this teaching was being expounded here, five hundred gods and humans conceived the aspiration for enlightenment.
And I was rendered speechless.
Therefore, Blessed One, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire after his illness.
Then the Blessed One addressed the bodhisattva Jagatīndhara:
“Go, Jagatindhara, as one who inquires after the illness of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti. Jagatindhara replied,
“Lord, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire after his illness.”
For what reason? I recall, Blessed One, that on one occasion I was staying in my own monastery.

Then Māra, the Evil One, surrounded by twelve thousand apsarases and disguised as Śakra, approached me with the sounding of musical instruments and songs; having bowed his head at my feet, he stood to one side with his retinue, placing me at their head.
I recognized him, thinking: "This is Śakra, the Lord of the Devas."
I said this to him:
"Welcome to you, Kauśika;
you must remain vigilant regarding all delights of sensual pleasure."
"You should take as your essence the frequent contemplation of impermanence regarding this body, life, and wealth.
He then said to me:
"O noble man, accept from me these twelve thousand celestial nymphs."
"Let these be your attendants.
To him I said this:
"Kauśika, do not invite the Śramaṇas, sons of the Śākyas, with unsuitable things."
Thinking, "Indeed, these are not suitable for us," this conversation was underway when the Licchavi Vimalakīrti approached.
He said this to me:
"Do not, noble son, conceive the notion that this is Śakra;
this is Māra the Evil One, who has approached you with the intention of harassing you."
"This is not Śakra.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said this to Māra, the Evil One:
"Evil One, give these goddesses to us."
"These belong to us, not to the Śākya-son ascetics," [said they].
Then Māra, the Evil One, became afraid, terrified, and agitated.
Thinking, "I must not be outshone by the Licchavi Vimalakīrti," he wished to disappear; yet, despite displaying all his supernatural powers, he was unable to vanish.
He heard a voice from the sky:
"O Evil One, give back these celestial nymphs to this virtuous man; only then will you be able to go to your own abode."
Then Māra, terrified and trembling, unwillingly surrendered those apsarases to him.
Having accepted them, Vimalakīrti said this to the apsarases: "You have been surrendered to me by Māra, the Evil One."
"Now, generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Having then delivered to them a discourse conducive to that and ripening for enlightenment, he caused them to generate the mind set upon enlightenment.
He spoke to them thus:
Now that you have generated the mind of awakening,
you should henceforth delight in the joy of the garden of the Dharma,
not in the joy of sensual desires.
They asked: "And what, moreover, is the delight in the garden of the Dharma?
He replied: "The delight in unshakable faith in the Buddha, and the delight in listening to the Dharma."
Delight in serving the Saṅgha, delight in showing respect and service toward one's teachers,
and delight in renunciation from the three realms.
Delight in not relying on sense objects;
delight in contemplating the aggregates as murderers and impermanent; delight in comparing the elements to venomous serpents.
Delight in solitude within the sense-bases as if in an empty village; delight in protecting the mind of awakening; and delight in acting for the benefit of sentient beings.
Delight in sharing through generosity, delight in steadfastness regarding the precepts,
and delight in patience and self-control.

Delight in the cultivation of wholesome qualities through vigor; delight in the preparatory exercises for the meditative concentrations; and delight in the radiance that dispels afflictions through wisdom.
Delight in the vastness of awakening, delight in the subduing of Māra,
and delight in the destruction of the afflictions.
Delight in purifying the buddha-field; delight in accumulating all roots of virtue for the sake of perfecting the primary and secondary marks;
and delight in not being terrified upon hearing the profound Dharma.
Delight in mastering the three gates of liberation,
delight in taking nirvana as one's object,
and delight in adorning the seat of enlightenment.

Nor is there delight in attaining [the goal] at an improper time; delight in associating with people of similar character; and delight in being free from malice and resentment toward those of dissimilar character.
Delight in attending upon spiritual friends, delight in avoiding evil friends,
and delight in the joy and gladness of the Dharma.
Delight in the means of attraction, and delight in the practice of the factors conducive to awakening through heedfulness;
in this way, a bodhisattva becomes one who delights in the pleasure of the garden of the Dharma.
Then Māra, the Evil One, said this to those celestial maidens: "Come, let us now go to our own abode.
They replied as follows:
"We have now been surrendered by you to this householder;
we must henceforth take delight in the pleasure grove of the Dharma, not in the pleasure of sensual desires."
Then Māra, the Evil One, said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti: "Householder, give up these celestial nymphs;
for Bodhisattvas, Mahāsattvas, are those who renounce all their possessions."
Vimalakīrti said:
"Let them go; depart, O Evil One!"
"May the righteous aspirations of all sentient beings be fulfilled.
Then those celestial nymphs, having paid homage to Vimalakīrti, said this:
"Householder, how shall we remain in the abode of Māra?"
He said: "Sisters, there is a gateway to the Dharma called the 'Inexhaustible Lamp. Practice therein. What, then, is it?"
Sisters, it is just as when hundreds of thousands of lamps are lit from a single lamp of oil;
yet there is no diminution of that original lamp.
In the same way, sisters, a single bodhisattva establishes many hundreds of thousands of beings in enlightenment.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva’s mindfulness of mind does not diminish,
nor does it decline; rather, it increases.
In this way, to whatever extent one announces and teaches all wholesome qualities to others, to that same extent one increases in all wholesome qualities.
This is the Dharma-door called "The Inexhaustible Lamp."
In that regard, while remaining in the abode of Māra, you must cause immeasurable sons of gods and apsarases to take delight in the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*).
In this way, you will be grateful to the Tathāgata and will become a source of sustenance for all sentient beings.
Then those celestial maidens bowed their heads at the feet of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti and departed together with Māra.
"Lord, these were the extraordinary miraculous transformations of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti that I did not recognize."
"Therefore, Blessed One, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire about his illness.
Then the Blessed One addressed Sudatta, the son of a merchant:
"Go, noble son, as an inquirer after the illness of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti."
Sudatta also said: "Lord, I am not able to go as an inquirer after the illness of that good man.
For what reason? Because—"
"I recall, Blessed One,
that in my own paternal home I performed a great sacrifice;
I gave gifts to all the poor and suffering, and to all the śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, the destitute, the beggars, and those who came seeking alms."
"For seven days I have been performing a great sacrifice.
On the seventh day, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti entered that hall of the great sacrifice and said this to me:
'O son of a merchant, a sacrifice should not be performed in the manner that you are performing it.'"
"A Dharma-sacrifice is to be performed by you;
what use have you for a sacrifice of material things?
To him I said this:
"But how, then, should the Dharma-sacrifice be performed? He said this to me:
"By that Dharma-sacrifice through which all sentient beings are ripened simultaneously, without first or last."
This is the sacrifice of Dharma.
Furthermore, what is it?
It is great loving-kindness brought forth through the aspects of awakening.
Great compassion is brought forth by the gathering of the true Dharma;
great sympathetic joy is brought forth by taking the gladness of all sentient beings as its object; great equanimity is brought forth by the gathering of primordial wisdom.
The perfection of generosity is accomplished through tranquility and self-restraint; the perfection of ethical discipline is accomplished through the ripening of beings who are immoral;
the perfection of patience is accomplished through the realization of the selflessness of phenomena.
The perfection of vigor is brought forth by the factors of enlightenment;
the perfection of meditation is brought forth by the seclusion of body and mind;
the perfection of wisdom is brought forth by the knowledge of omniscience.

The cultivation of emptiness is brought forth by the ripening of all sentient beings; the cultivation of the signless is brought forth by the refinement of conditioned phenomena; the cultivation of the wishless is brought forth by intentional rebirth.
His strength and prowess are brought forth through the upholding of the true Dharma; his life-faculty is brought forth through the articles of attraction;
and his freedom from pride is brought forth by acting as a servant and a disciple to all sentient beings.
The acquisition of body, life, and enjoyments is brought forth from extracting the essence from the insubstantial;
mindfulness is brought forth by means of the six recollections;
and the resolute intention is brought forth by means of the qualities that inspire affection.
Purity of livelihood brought forth by correct practice; attendance upon the noble ones brought forth by the cultivation of serene confidence and joy;
and mental composure brought forth by the absence of resentment toward those who are not noble.
The resolute intention brought forth by going forth;
skill in learning brought forth by practice;
dwelling in the forest brought forth by the penetration of the dharma free from affliction.
Secluded meditation is brought forth by the attainment of the Buddha’s wisdom;
the stage of the practitioner of yoga is brought forth by the application of liberating all sentient beings from their afflictions;
and the ripening of sentient beings is brought forth by the accumulation of the primary and secondary marks.
The accumulation of merit is brought forth by the adornment of the buddha-field;
the accumulation of wisdom is brought forth by the teaching of the Dharma according to the mental activities and inclinations of all sentient beings;
and the accumulation of insight is brought forth by the knowledge of the single principle that neither brings in nor casts out any phenomena.

This, noble son, is the Dharma-sacrifice: it is the accumulation of all roots of merit brought forth by the abandonment of all afflictions, all obstructions, and all unwholesome states; it is the emergence of all factors conducive to awakening, brought forth by the realization of the wisdom of omniscience and all wholesome states.
"In that sacrifice of Dharma where Bodhisattvas are established, they become performers of the desired sacrifice and worthy recipients of offerings for the world including its gods.
Thus, Lord, as that householder was teaching, two hundred brahmins from that assembly of brahmins conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
And I, having attained a sense of wonder and serene faith, bowed at the feet of that good man and, taking off a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand [pieces] from my neck, gave it to him.
He did not accept the pearl necklace offered by them.
I said this to him:
"Please accept this."
"Give it to whomever you have favor toward," he said.
He took that pearl necklace and divided it into two parts;
one portion was given to the city pauper who was despised by all the people there at the sacrificial hall.
And the second portion was given to the Tathāgata Duṣprasaha;
and so the entire assembly saw that world-system Marīci, that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha,
and that pearl necklace which, upon reaching the crown of Duṣprasaha’s head, appeared as a variegated gabled palace made of pearls.
It was beautiful to behold, quadrangular, with four pillars, perfectly symmetrical and well-proportioned.
Having displayed this miracle, he spoke these words:
"Whatever notion of a worthy recipient (dakṣiṇīya) a donor or master of charity has toward the Tathāgata, such a notion is held equally, without distinction, toward the poor of the city."
Giving with a mind of great compassion, without expectation of karmic fruition—
this is the fulfillment of the Dharma-sacrifice.
Thereupon, that poor man of the city, having seen this miracle, [was filled with wonder].
Having heard this teaching of the Dharma,
he has resolved his mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Therefore, O Blessed One, I am not able to go to that good man to inquire after his illness.
Thus, all those bodhisattva mahāsattvas each set forth their own respective expositions; and as for the conversations they had with that good man,
they were unable to depart.
The third chapter, titled "The Question on the Dismissal of the Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas."
Thereupon, the Blessed One addressed Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
“Mañjuśrī, go to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti to inquire about his illness.
Mañjuśrī replied:
Moreover, Lord, that Licchavi Vimalakīrti is difficult to approach;
he has entered into profound methods and eloquence,
and is skilled in the deployment of words both individually and collectively.
Possessing unimpeded eloquence,
with incomparable intelligence toward all sentient beings,
he was proficient in all the activities of a bodhisattva.

He has thoroughly entered all the secret abodes of all bodhisattvas and all buddhas; he sports with the great supernormal knowledges that are skilled in turning back from all the abodes of Māra; and he has attained the supreme perfection of the domain of the non-dual, indivisible dharmadhātu.
He is the expounder of the Dharma that reveals the infinite arrays of forms within the single array of the dharma-realm;
he is skilled in the wisdom that brings about the mastery of the arrays of the faculties of all sentient beings;
and he has reached the culmination of skill in means.
Having attained certainty regarding the questions,
he cannot be satisfied by a mere slight armor.
Nevertheless, I shall go forth through the empowerment of the Buddha.
In this regard, I shall explain according to my ability and according to my strength.
Then, it occurred to those bodhisattvas in that assembly, as well as to those śrāvakas, those Śakras, Brahmās, and Lokapālas, and those sons of the gods:
"Undoubtedly, there will be a great discourse and discussion on the Dharma there."
Where Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and that good man were both conversing,
there eight thousand bodhisattvas, about five hundred śrāvakas, many Śakras, Brahmās, and world-protectors, and many hundreds of thousands of sons of gods followed after Mañjuśrī to hear the Dharma.

Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, surrounded by those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, those śrāvakas, those Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and sons of gods, entered the great city of Vaiśālī. Then, this thought occurred to Vimalakīrti:
"Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta is coming with a great retinue;
what if I were to empower this house to be empty?
Thereupon, he empowered that house to be empty, cleared of its doorkeepers.
No beds, stools, or seats were visible there, except for a single bed upon which he himself, being ill, had ascended and was lying.
Then Mañjuśrī, together with his retinue, approached the residence of Vimalakīrti.
Having approached, he entered;
he saw that house empty and devoid of gatekeepers,
and there he saw no couches or stools except for a single couch.
Where Vimalakīrti was lying,
the Licchavi Vimalakīrti beheld Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; having seen him, he spoke as follows:
"Welcome, Mañjuśrī! Welcome, Mañjuśrī! It is a sight to behold the one who has not come, and whom we have never before seen or heard.
Mañjuśrī said: "It is even so, householder, just as you say."
He who has come will not come again;
and he who has gone will not go again.
For what reason? Because:
Neither the arrival of one who has arrived is perceived,
nor the departure of one who has departed; and that which has been seen is not to be seen again.
Moreover, O noble sir, is it well with you? Are you able to endure, are you able to maintain yourself?
Are your physical elements disturbed by wind?
I hope your illness is departing and not increasing.

The Blessed One asks after your freedom from affliction, your freedom from distress, your freedom from sickness, your ease of movement, your vigor, your strength, your well-being, your blamelessness, and your state of dwelling in comfort.
“Householder, where did this onset of your illness originate?
For how long have you had this illness? And when will it subside?”
Vimalakīrti said: "Mañjuśrī, for as long as ignorance and the craving for existence have existed, for that long has this illness of mine existed.
And when all sentient beings shall be free from illness, then my illness will be stilled."
For what reason?
Mañjuśrī, for a bodhisattva, saṃsāra has sentient beings as its basis;
and sickness is dependent upon saṃsāra.
When all sentient beings have become free from illness, then the bodhisattva will be free from illness.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as if the only son of a merchant were to fall ill;
his mother and father would also fall ill on account of him.
And those two would remain in a state of suffering as long as that only son of theirs had not been freed from his illness.
In the same way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva’s love for all sentient beings is like that for an only son;
he becomes ill with the illness of sentient beings.
He is free from disease because of the health of sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, as to what you asked— "From where does the sickness of the bodhisattvas arise?"— the sickness of the bodhisattvas arises from great compassion.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Householder, your house is empty, and you have no attendant at all."
He said: "Mañjuśrī, even all buddha-fields are empty.
He asked: "By what are they empty?
He replied: "They are empty by means of emptiness."
He asked: "What is the emptiness of emptiness?
He replied: "The non-conceptualization of emptiness is the emptiness of emptiness.
He asked: "But can emptiness be conceptualized?"
He said: "That by which one might conceptualize is itself empty;
moreover, emptiness does not conceptualize emptiness.
He asked: "Householder, from where is emptiness to be sought?"
He said: "Mañjuśrī, emptiness is to be sought within the sixty-two types of views. He asked: "But where are the sixty-two types of views to be sought?
He replied: "They are to be sought within the liberation of the Tathāgata."
He asked: "Furthermore, from where should the liberation of the Tathāgata be sought?
He replied: "It should be sought from the mental activities of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, as for what you ask: "Who is your attendant?"
All Māras and all proponents of opposing doctrines are my attendants.
For what reason?
Because Māras are those who praise cyclic existence (saṃsāra).
Furthermore, for a bodhisattva, cyclic existence is an attendant;
yet while others who propound various doctrines praise their own views,
the bodhisattva does not waver from any of those views.
"Therefore, all Māras and all proponents of opposing doctrines are my attendants.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Householder, what kind of illness is this of yours?"
He said: "It is invisible and non-demonstrable.
He asked: "Is this illness associated with the body or associated with the mind?
He replied: "It is not associated with the body, because of the body's isolation."
It is not associated with the mind because of the illusory nature of the mind.
He said: "Householder, there are these four elements. Which four?"
Namely, the earth element, the water element, the fire element, and the wind element.
Among these, which element afflicts him?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī, whatever element constitutes the disease of all sentient beings, by that I am afflicted."
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, how should a bodhisattva console a sick bodhisattva?
Mañjuśrī replied:
"By means of the impermanence of the body, yet not by way of weariness or revulsion."
Through the suffering nature of the body, yet not through longing for nirvāṇa;
through the selflessness of the body, yet through the ripening of sentient beings;
through the tranquility of the body, yet not through ultimate quiescence.
By confessing all misdeeds, yet not through transmigration;
by feeling compassion for other sentient beings who are afflicted because of one's own affliction; and by recollecting the suffering of the limits of the past.
by means of recollecting the performance of the welfare of sentient beings, by means of bringing the roots of virtue into manifestation,
and by means of primordial purity;
"Because you do not become weary and because you always exert vigor, you shall become a king of physicians who pacifies all diseases."
In this way, a bodhisattva should console a sick bodhisattva.
Mañjuśrī said:
"Noble son, how should a sick bodhisattva settle his own mind?"
Vimalakīrti said:
"In this regard, Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should thus settle his own mind:
'This illness has arisen from the origination of karma produced by false inversions since the beginningless past; it has arisen from the afflictions of unreal conceptualization.'"
Furthermore, here no phenomenon whatsoever is apprehended in the ultimate sense to which this illness belongs.
For what reason?
Because this physical body is composed of the four great elements.
There is no owner of these elements, nor is there any one who brings them forth;
for this physical aggregate is without self.
This which is called "disease" is not found in ultimate reality.
Except for attachment to a self;

rather, not being fully settled in a self, we shall dwell having thoroughly understood the root of disease. Therefore, having cast aside the perception of a self, the perception of phenomena (dharma) should be produced.
This body is a collection of phenomena;
only phenomena arise as they arise,
and only phenomena cease as they cease.
And those phenomena do not intend toward one another, nor do they know;
nor does it occur to them as they arise, "We are arising," nor does it occur to them as they cease, "We are ceasing."
Therefore, regarding the very notion of "dharmas," one should generate this thought:
"Even this notion of dharmas is a perversion;
and perversion is a great malady."
I must become free from disease,
and I must apply myself to the abandonment of disease.
In that regard, what is the abandonment of disease?
This is the abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine.
And what is that abandonment of the notions of "I" and "mine"?
It is this: the departure from duality.
In that regard, what is the departure from duality?
It is this: the manifestation [of consciousness] internally and externally.
In that regard, what is the internal and external manifestation?
That is to say, it is immovability and unshakeability through equanimity.
And what is equanimity? It is the equanimity of the self and the equanimity of nirvāṇa.
For what reason?
Both of these are empty, namely, the self and nirvana.
By what are these empty? They are empty by way of the utterance of a name; both of these are likewise unestablished.
That is to say, the self and nirvāṇa.
For one who sees them as equal, no distinction between illness and emptiness should be made;
illness itself is emptiness.
That feeling should be experienced as something unknown;
yet he should not personally realize the cessation of feeling.
As long as the qualities of a Buddha are not fully perfected, both types of feeling must not be abandoned.
Furthermore, one should not fail to generate great compassion toward sentient beings born in the miserable realms;
rather, we shall act in such a way that we will remove the disease of these beings through this very improper reflection.
Yet, we shall neither introduce any dharma to them nor remove any from them.
Furthermore, for the sake of fully understanding the causal basis from which disease arises, we shall teach the Dharma concerning them.
And what is that causal basis?
It is this: the causal basis of objective grasping (*adhyālambana-nidāna*).
To the extent that one takes up an object of focus as a cause, to that extent it is a cause of disease.
And what is it that one takes up as an object?
One takes the triple world as an object of apprehension. What is the thorough knowledge of that through such apprehension?
It is this: the non-apprehension of the object.
For that which is not perceived is not taken as an object. And what is it that one does not perceive?
One does not perceive both views.
That which consists of the view of self and the view of others is called "non-apprehension.
For in this way, Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should settle his own mind for the sake of abandoning old age, sickness, death, and rebirth.
And thus, Mañjuśrī, if the awakening of bodhisattvas were not to exist,
would their exertion not indeed be purposeless?
Just as those who destroy their enemies are called heroes, so too [is the effort of the bodhisattvas].
In the same way, because they pacify the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death, they are called "bodhisattvas.
That sick bodhisattva should reflect in this way:
"Just as my own sickness is unreal and non-existent, so too the sickness of all sentient beings is unreal and non-existent."
As he reflects in this way, a great compassion for sentient beings arises that does not fall into the view of seeking personal benefit;
rather, a great compassion for sentient beings arises through his application to abandoning adventitious afflictions.
Why is that?
For it is through great compassion that has fallen into the view of [perceiving] benefits that a bodhisattva experiences weariness with rebirths;
however, through great compassion that is free from the obsession (paryutthāna) of the view of benefits, a bodhisattva does not experience weariness with rebirths. Thus he is reborn.
Nor does he arise while possessed by the outbursts of views;
arising with a mind free from such outbursts, he is born already liberated, he is produced already liberated.
Being thus born already liberated and produced already liberated, he is capable and empowered to teach the Dharma for the sake of the liberation from bondage of sentient beings who are bound.

As it was said by the Blessed One: "That one who is himself bound will liberate another from bondage—this is impossible. But that one who is himself liberated will liberate another from bondage—this is possible. Therefore, a bodhisattva should be liberated, not bound.
In that regard, what is bondage and what is liberation?
For a bodhisattva, the grasping at the realms of existence through a lack of skillful means is bondage.
Going through the realms of existence by means of skillful means is liberation;
for a bodhisattva, the relishing of meditative absorptions and concentrations through a lack of skillful means is bondage,
whereas the relishing of meditative absorptions and concentrations through skillful means is liberation.
Wisdom not embraced by skillful means is bondage;
wisdom embraced by skillful means is liberation. Skillful means not embraced by wisdom is bondage.
Skillful means embraced by wisdom is liberation.
In this regard, what is wisdom not embraced by skillful means that constitutes bondage?
It is the contemplation of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness [without the accompaniment of compassion].
Nor is there the realization of the primary marks and secondary characteristics, the adornment of the Buddha-field, and the ripening of sentient beings.
This wisdom, when not embraced by skillful means, is bondage.
In that regard, what is wisdom embraced by skillful means that is liberation?

That which consists of the mental resolve for the primary marks, the secondary characteristics, the adornment of the buddha-field, and the ripening of sentient beings, together with mastery over emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—
this is wisdom embraced by skillful means, which is liberation. In that regard, what is skillful means not embraced by wisdom, which is bondage?

This is as follows: for one who remains established in all views, afflictions, outbursts, latent tendencies, attachments, and aversions, the undertaking of all roots of virtue without dedicating them toward awakening—this is skillful means uncomprehended by wisdom, which is bondage.
In that regard, what is skillful means comprehended by wisdom, which is liberation?

This is the undertaking of all roots of virtue by one who has abandoned all views, afflictions, outbursts, latent tendencies, attachments, and aversions, and having dedicated them toward awakening, remaining free from grasping at them.
This is the bodhisattva’s liberation consisting of skillful means embraced by wisdom.
In this regard, Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should reflect upon these phenomena in this way.
That which consists of the contemplation of the body, the mind, and illness as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self—
this is his wisdom. Furthermore, that he does not become weary through the avoidance of physical illness is [his skillful means].
Being devoted to the application of benefiting sentient beings, he does not obstruct cyclic existence;
this is his skillful means.
Furthermore, that which consists in examining the mutual succession of the body’s disease and the mind— neither as something new nor as something old—
is his wisdom (*prajñā*).
Moreover, that which does not transcend the absolute pacification and cessation of the body’s disease and the mind is [his insight].
This is his means.
Mañjuśrī, a sick bodhisattva should thus settle his mind;
yet he should not abide in either that settling or the non-settling.
For what reason?
For if one were to abide in non-conciliation, that would be the way of the foolish;
but if one were to abide in conciliation, that would be the way of the śrāvakas.
Therefore, a bodhisattva should not abide in conviction. That which is a state of non-abiding is the domain of a bodhisattva;
that which is neither the domain of ordinary beings nor the domain of noble ones is [the domain of a bodhisattva].
This is the range of the bodhisattva:
that which is the range of saṃsāra, yet not the range of the afflictions;
this is the range of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of the contemplation of nirvāṇa, yet not the domain of ultimate parinirvāṇa— this is the domain of the bodhisattva. That which is the domain of beholding the four māras, yet the domain of having transcended the entire range of the māras— this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of seeking the wisdom of omniscience, yet not the domain of attaining that wisdom at an improper time;
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of the knowledge of the four truths, yet not the domain of penetrating the truths at an improper time— this is the domain of the bodhisattva. That which is the domain of internal investigation, yet the domain of intentionally taking up rebirth in existence— this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of the contemplation of non-arising, yet is not the domain of entering the fixed course of determination;
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of dependent origination and yet the domain free from all views— this is the domain of the bodhisattva. That which is the domain of socializing with all sentient beings and yet not the domain of the latent tendencies of the afflictions— this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of seclusion, yet not the domain of relying on the exhaustion of body and mind;
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
That which is the domain of the three realms yet not the domain of the differentiation of the dharma-realm—
this is the domain of the bodhisattva;
that which is the domain of emptiness yet the domain of the pursuit of qualities in all their aspects.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of the signless (*animitta*) and yet the domain of mental application directed toward the objective of liberating sentient beings;
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
That which is the sphere of the wishless (*apraṇihita*) and yet the sphere of intentionally manifesting existence and the realms of rebirth (*saṃcintyabhavagati*),
this is the sphere of the bodhisattva;
that which is the sphere of non-conditioning (*anabhisaṃskāra*) and yet the sphere of never ceasing the conditioning of all roots of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).
This is the sphere of the bodhisattva:
that which is the sphere of the six perfections and the sphere of reaching the further shore regarding the mental activities of all sentient beings—
this is the sphere of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of the six recollections, yet not the domain of the exhaustion of all outflows— this is the domain of the bodhisattva. That which is the domain of establishing the true Dharma, yet not the domain of taking recourse to false paths— this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
