that which is the domain of the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) yet is not the domain of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
This is the domain of the bodhisattva.
That which is the domain of the four immeasurables, yet not the domain of attaining rebirth in the Brahma-world—
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of meditative absorptions, concentrations, and attainments, yet not the domain of rebirth through the power of those concentrations and attainments— [this is the domain of the bodhisattva].
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of the applications of mindfulness, yet is not a domain characterized by excessive preoccupation with the body, feelings, mind, or phenomena;
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.

That which is the domain of the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*) yet not the domain of perceiving the duality of the wholesome and unwholesome— this is the domain of the bodhisattva. That which is the domain of accomplishing the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) and the domain of mastery over effortless psychic power— this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of the five faculties and the domain of the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of all sentient beings—
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.
That which is the sphere of activity consisting in being established in the five powers and the sphere of activity consisting in the manifestation of the ten powers of a Tathāgata—
this is the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.

That which is the sphere of activity consisting in the perfection of the seven factors of awakening and the sphere of activity consisting in skill in the knowledge that discriminates between types of intelligence— this is the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva.
This is the range of the bodhisattva:
that which is the range of abiding in the path and the range of not taking recourse to wrong paths—
this is the range of the bodhisattva.
That which is the sphere of seeking the equipment for tranquility and insight, yet is not the sphere of falling into absolute peace;

that which is the sphere of investigating all phenomena as having the characteristic of non-arising, yet is the sphere of perfecting the adornment of the Buddha-body with the primary marks and secondary signs— this is the sphere of the bodhisattva.
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
that which is the domain of manifesting as a śrāvaka or pratyekabuddha for an eon, and yet the domain of never abandoning the qualities of a Buddha—
this is the domain of the bodhisattva.

That which is the sphere of activity consisting in following all phenomena that have attained the nature of ultimate purity, and the sphere of activity consisting in manifesting the modes of conduct for all sentient beings according to their inclinations— this is the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva. That which is the sphere of activity consisting in the contemplation of all buddha-fields as having the nature of space, being ultimately without dissolution or evolution, and the sphere of activity consisting in manifesting the arrays of qualities of buddha-fields through various and manifold arrangements— [this is the sphere of activity of a bodhisattva].
This is the domain of the bodhisattva:
both the domain of manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma and the great parinirvāṇa, and the domain of not abandoning the conduct of a bodhisattva—
this too is the domain of the bodhisattva.

While this exposition was being taught, among those sons of the gods who had come together with Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, the minds of eight thousand sons of the gods were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
The fourth chapter: On Consoling the Sick.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Where will these bodhisattvas sit, as well as these great śrāvakas?"
"No seats are found here.
Then, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, knowing the thought in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, have you come seeking the Dharma, or are you seeking a seat?"
He said: "We have come seeking the Dharma, not seeking a seat.
Vimalakīrti said: "In that case, Reverend Śāriputra, he who seeks the Dharma does not seek his own body."
How much less, then, would he be one who seeks a seat?
Venerable Śāriputra, he who is a seeker of the Dharma does not seek form, feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.
One who seeks the Dharma does not seek the aggregates, elements, or sense bases;
one who seeks the Dharma does not become a seeker of the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm.
He does not seek attachment to the Buddha, nor does he seek attachment to the Dharma or the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, he who seeks the Dharma—
He does not seek the full understanding of suffering, nor the abandonment of its origin, nor the realization of its cessation, nor the cultivation of the path.
Why is that?
Because the Dharma is non-proliferated and beyond syllables.

In this regard, whoever conceptualizes, thinking, "I shall fully understand suffering, I shall abandon its origin, I shall realize cessation, and I shall cultivate the path," is not one who seeks the Dharma;
such a person seeks conceptual proliferation.
For the Dharma, Venerable Śāriputra, is utterly tranquil. In this regard, those who course in arising and ceasing are not seekers of the Dharma, nor are they seekers of seclusion.
They are seekers of arising and ceasing;
for the Dharma is indeed dustless and free from dust. In this regard, those who cling to any dharma—even to nirvana—[are not followers of the Dharma].
They do not seek the Dharma; they seek defilement. For the Dharma is beyond the sphere of sensory objects.
Those who are reckoned as objects of the senses are not seekers of the Dharma;
they are seekers of sense-objects.
Dharma is neither grasping nor relinquishing;
those who either grasp at or release phenomena do not seek the true meaning of Dharma.
They are seekers of grasping and relinquishing;
yet the Dharma is without abode.
Those who delight in an abode—
They do not seek the Dharma;
they seek the *ālaya*.
The Dharma is signless (*nirnimitta*).
Those whose consciousness follows after signs are not seekers of the Dharma;
they are seekers of signs.
The Dharma is non-dwelling;
whoever dwells together with the Dharma does not seek the Dharma.
They are seekers of companionship;
the Dharma is that which has not been seen, heard, thought, or cognized.
Those who practice regarding what has been seen, heard, thought, and cognized [are not true seekers].
They do not seek the Dharma;
they seek what has been seen, heard, thought, and cognized.
Venerable Śāriputra, the Dharma is unconditioned and free from the conditioned.
Those whose sphere is the conditioned are not seekers of the Dharma;
they are seekers of the grasping of the conditioned.
Therefore, Reverend Śāriputra, one who wishes to be a seeker of the Dharma here must be a seeker of no-dharma.
While this teaching of the Dharma was being expounded, the Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena was purified in five hundred sons of the gods.
Then, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed Mañjuśrī, the Crown Prince:

"Mañjuśrī, you travel on a tour of buddha-fields throughout hundreds of thousands of incalculable buddha-fields in the ten directions. In which buddha-field have you seen lion thrones that are most excellent and endowed with every virtue?
When this was said, Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta replied to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti as follows:
"Noble son, in the eastern direction, beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in thirty-six Ganges rivers, there is a world-system named Merudhvajā.
Therein dwells, remains, and maintains his life the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Merupradīparāja.
The physical body of that Tathāgata is eighty-four hundred thousand yojanas in height."
The lion throne of that Blessed One was six million eight hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
the bodies of those bodhisattvas were four million yojanas in height;
and the lion thrones of those bodhisattvas were three million four hundred thousand yojanas in extent.
In the world-system Merudhvajā, within the buddha-field of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Merupradīparāja, there were lion thrones endowed with every excellence and all virtuous qualities.
Then, at that time, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti focused his attention in such a manner and performed such a miraculous feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhy-abhisaṃskāra*).
Then, thirty-two hundred thousand lion-thrones were sent by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Merupradīparāja, from the world-system Merudhvaja; they were so high, so wide,
and so beautiful to behold as to be unprecedented for those bodhisattvas, those great śrāvakas, those Śakras, Brahmās, Lokapālas, and sons of gods.
Having come through the air above, they settled in the residence of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti;
and that house appeared to be so vast that those three million two hundred thousand variegated lion-thrones could fit within it without crowding.
Nor was there any obstruction made to the great city of Vaiśālī, nor to Jambudvīpa, nor was there any obstruction to the four-continent world-system.
All of them appeared exactly as they were before, and so too after.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said this to the crown prince Mañjuśrī:
"Mañjuśrī, sit upon the lion-throne together with these bodhisattvas."
"And assume such physical forms that they may be suitable for those lion thrones.
Then, those bodhisattvas who had attained the superknowledges (*abhijñā*) assumed physical forms forty-two hundred thousand *yojanas* in height and sat down upon those lion thrones;
however, those bodhisattvas who were beginners (*ādikarmika*) were unable to sit upon those lion thrones.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Sit, venerable Śāriputra, upon this lion-throne.
He replied: "I am unable to sit, O noble sir, for these lion-thrones are so high and elevated."
He said: "In that case, Venerable Śāriputra, pay homage to that very Blessed One, the Tathāgata Merupradīparāja;
then you will be able to sit down.
Thereupon, those great śrāvakas paid homage to that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Merupradīparāja.
Thereupon, they sat down upon those lion-thrones.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"It is marvelous, noble son, that within this very small house there are these thousands of lion-thrones, so high, so magnificent, and so variegated!"
Nor was there any obstruction made to the great city of Vaiśālī, nor to Jambudvīpa, nor to the villages, cities, market towns, districts, kingdoms, and royal capitals.
There was no obstruction for the world of the four great continents,
nor was any obstruction created for the gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, or mahoragas;
they appeared exactly as they were before, just as they were afterward.
Vimalakīrti said:
"Reverend Śāriputra, there is a liberation of the Tathāgatas and Bodhisattvas called 'Inconceivable.
Established in this inconceivable liberation, a Bodhisattva can place Mount Sumeru—the king of mountains, so high, so lofty, so towering, and so vast—within the shell of a mustard seed."
One should cause it to enter;
yet one should not increase the size of a mustard seed's pod,
nor should one diminish Mount Sumeru.
And he should demonstrate that feat in such a way that neither the gods of the Four Great Kings nor those of the Thirty-three would know, "Where have we been cast?
while other beings who are to be converted by means of supernatural power would know and see that Sumeru, the king of mountains, has entered into the interior of a mustard seed.
"Venerable Śāriputra, this is the entrance into the domain of the inconceivable liberation of bodhisattvas.

Furthermore, venerable Śāriputra, a bodhisattva established in the inconceivable liberation could take the mass of water in the four great oceans and pour it into a single pore of his skin, yet there would be no suffering for the fish, turtles, crocodiles, frogs, or any other aquatic creatures."
Nor would it occur to the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, or asuras, "Into what have we been cast?
and that action would be perceived [only by the practitioner],
and no sentient being whatsoever would be harmed or afflicted.
And having grasped this trichiliocosm world-system like a potter’s wheel and whirled it around in his right hand, he might cast it into world-systems as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges;
yet the sentient beings would not know: "Where have we been taken? or "From where have we come?"
Furthermore, having brought them back, he should place them in their respective positions;
yet they would not perceive any coming or going,
and that action would still be visible.
Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, there are beings who are to be disciplined through an immeasurable cycle of existence,
and there are those who are to be disciplined through a brief cycle of existence.

In this regard, a bodhisattva established in the inconceivable liberation, by virtue of the power of disciplining those beings who are to be disciplined through an immeasurable cycle of existence, may manifest the passing of an eon as merely seven nights.

For the sake of training those beings who are to be disciplined by a brief cycle of existence, he may, by the power of his mastery over discipline, cause them to perceive a single eon as having passed in seven nights.

Therein, those beings to be trained by an immeasurable cycle of existence will perceive seven nights as an eon having passed, while those beings to be trained by a brief cycle of existence will perceive an eon as seven nights having passed. Thus, a bodhisattva established in the inconceivable liberation displays the magnificent arrays of qualities of all buddha-fields within a single buddha-field.
Even having established all sentient beings upon the palm of his right hand, he could traverse them by means of psychic power born of mind;
and he could manifest himself in all buddha-fields,
yet he would not move from even a single field.
Whatever offerings to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are being performed throughout the ten directions, he would display them all within a single pore;
and as many moons, suns, and star-forms as there are in the ten directions, [he would likewise display them].
He would display all of those within a single pore of his skin;
and as many whirlwinds as blow throughout the ten directions, he would cause them all to enter through the opening of his mouth.
Furthermore, his body would not be scattered,

nor would the grasses and trees in that buddha-field be bent down. And as for those buddha-fields in the ten directions that are being consumed by the fire at the end of the eon, [he would not be affected].
He would cast even that entire mass of fire into his own mouth;
and whatever deed he was required to perform, that too he would do.
And having crossed over from this world downward as many Buddha-fields as there are tens of millions of grains of sand in the Ganges River,
he might lift up a single Buddha-field and establish it in the upward direction across as many Buddha-fields as there are tens of millions of grains of sand in the Ganges River—
just as, for example, a strong man might toss a jujube leaf with the point of a needle.
Vkn 5.16 Thus, a bodhisattva established in the liberation of the unconditioned may empower all sentient beings to take on the forms of universal monarchs and so forth.
Vkn 5.17 Furthermore, whatever manifestations of sound and designations of sound there are throughout the ten directions,
he empowers them all— whether belonging to inferior, middling, or superior beings— to be composed of the melodic resonance of the voice of all Buddhas.
Then, from that sound of vocalization, one should cause the sounds of the words "impermanence," "suffering," "emptiness," and "non-self" to issue forth;
and by whatever modes of description the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, teach the Dharma in the ten directions, those very sounds of vocalization one should cause to issue forth from it.
"Venerable Śāriputra, this is but a brief description of the entry into the range of those bodhisattvas who are established in the inconceivable liberation.

Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, for an eon, or the remainder of an eon, or even beyond that, I could continue to describe the entries into the range of the ranges of those bodhisattvas who are established in the inconceivable liberation."
Then, having heard this inconceivable liberation of the bodhisattvas, the elder Mahākāśyapa was struck with wonder and said to the elder Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, it is as if someone were to display all manner of forms before a man blind from birth;
yet that man blind from birth would not see even a single form therein."

In the same way, Venerable Śāriputra, when this inconceivable liberation is being taught, all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are like those born blind, deprived of sight; they do not perceive even a single inconceivable cause. What wise person, having heard of this inconceivable liberation, would not resolve their mind upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment?
What more indeed shall we do, our faculties utterly impaired, like seeds that are scorched and destroyed, having become unfit vessels for this Mahāyāna?
Upon hearing this teaching of the Dharma, all the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, weeping, should make the trichiliocosm resound with their lamentation;
and all the Bodhisattvas, filled with joy upon hearing this inconceivable liberation, should accept it with their heads bowed in reverence.
One must generate the power of resolute conviction;
for one who possesses this resolute conviction in the inconceivable liberation, what can all the Māras do?
As the Elder Mahākāśyapa was delivering this instruction, thirty-two thousand sons of gods conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said to the Elder Mahākāśyapa:
"Venerable Mahākāśyapa, as many Māras as there are in the immeasurable world-systems throughout the ten directions who exercise the power of Māra,
for the most part they are all bodhisattvas established in the inconceivable liberation who, through skill in means, exercise the power of Māra for the sake of maturing sentient beings."

Venerable Mahākāśyapa, as many Bodhisattvas as there are in the immeasurable world-systems throughout the ten directions who are entreated by supplicants for their hands or feet, or their ears or nose, or their blood, sinews, bones, or marrow, or their eyes, or their heads— the crowns of their bodies— or their limbs and members, or their kingdoms, nations, and provinces, or their wives, sons, and daughters, or their male and female slaves.
Or horses, elephants, chariots, and vehicles; or gold, jewels, pearls, beryl, conch shells, crystals, coral, and various kinds of precious gems;
or food, drink, flavors, and garments—these are sought by squeezing [the donor] for alms.
For the most part, all those beggars were bodhisattvas established in the inconceivable liberation who, through skill in means, displayed this firmness of high resolve.
Why is that?
Because, Reverend Mahākāśyapa, those bodhisattvas, being of fierce asceticism, display themselves in such a manner.
For there is no power for an ordinary person, who has been deprived of any opportunity or occasion, to oppress a bodhisattva.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is just as a firefly has no power to overcome the radiance of the sun’s orb;
even so, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, an ordinary person who has been deprived of any opportunity by a bodhisattva has no power to approach him or to make a request.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa, it is just as this: a blow from a noble elephant that cannot be endured by a donkey;
even so, Venerable Mahākāśyapa, one who is not a bodhisattva cannot endure the oppression of a bodhisattva.
Only a bodhisattva can endure the oppression of a bodhisattva.
Venerable Mahākāśyapa, this is the entry into the power of skillful means and knowledge of those bodhisattvas who are established in the inconceivable liberation.
The Fifth Chapter: The Manifestation of the Inconceivable Liberation.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"How, O noble son, should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī, it is just as if a wise man were to look at the moon reflected in water."
In this way, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as one might behold the reflection of a face in the surface of a mirror,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Just as, Mañjuśrī, there is water in a mirage, so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Just as, Mañjuśrī, a magician might regard a person created by magic, [so should he regard all sentient beings].
In this way, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as the sound of an echo,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.

Mañjuśrī, just as there is a mass of clouds in the sky, so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings. Mañjuśrī, just as is the prior limit of a lump of foam, [so should one contemplate all sentient beings].
In this way, a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as the arising and passing away of water bubbles occurs,
so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as one perceives the core of a plantain tree,
so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as there is the shifting of lightning, [so should he contemplate them].
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings; just as one regards the fifth element,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as one regards the seventh sense-base, so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, it is just like the appearance of form within the formless realms.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings; just as there is the production of sprouts from seeds that have been scorched,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as one might consider the hair of a frog's skin, so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as one might consider the pleasure of sensual play in a corpse, [so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings].
In this way, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as a stream-enterer regards the view of a self-identity, so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as a once-returner has only one more existence remaining,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as there is no entry into a womb for a non-returner, [so should he regard them].
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings; just as an arhat regards passion, hatred, and delusion,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as a bodhisattva who has attained patience has no thoughts of stinginess, immorality, malice, or violence,
so too should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, it is just as the Tathāgata has no latent tendencies of affliction (*kleśavāsanā*).
In this way, a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as a man born blind perceives forms,
so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as there are no inhalations for one who has entered the meditative attainment of cessation,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings. Mañjuśrī, just as the track of a bird in the sky [is non-existent], so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva should regard all sentient beings:
just as the emergence of the sexual organ of a eunuch [is non-existent],
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as a barren woman obtains a son,
so should a bodhisattva regard all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as the afflictions of one created by a Tathāgata’s emanation are non-arisen, [so should he regard them].
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings, just like the vision of one who has awakened from a dream.
In this way, a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as afflictions do not exist for one who does not conceptualize, so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings.
Mañjuśrī, just as there is the arising of a fire without fuel,
so should a bodhisattva contemplate all sentient beings. Mañjuśrī, just as there is a rebirth for one who has entered final nirvāṇa, [so should he contemplate them].
In this way, a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings.
For it is thus, Mañjuśrī, that a bodhisattva should contemplate all sentient beings.
He said: "Noble son, if a bodhisattva is to contemplate all sentient beings in this way,"
Furthermore, how does he possess great loving-kindness toward all sentient beings?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī, it is when a bodhisattva reflects thus:
'I must teach the Dharma to these sentient beings so that they may fully understand the Dharma in this way.'"

Therefore, his genuine loving-kindness that protects beings arises toward all sentient beings through non-objectification; his loving-kindness of tranquility through non-arising; and his loving-kindness free from feverish distress through freedom from afflictions.
Loving-kindness according to reality through the equality of the three times;
non-opposing loving-kindness through the absence of manifestation;
non-dual loving-kindness through the lack of conjunction between the internal and the external.
Unshakeable loving-kindness through its ultimate finality; firm loving-kindness through an intention as indestructible and solid as a diamond;
pure loving-kindness through natural purity.

The loving-kindness that is equal through its equality with space; the loving-kindness of an Arhat through the destruction of enemies; the loving-kindness of a Bodhisattva through the unflagging ripening of sentient beings.
The loving-kindness of the Tathāgata is through the realization of suchness;
the loving-kindness of the Buddha is through awakening sentient beings who are asleep;
the loving-kindness of the Self-Existent One is through self-awakening to enlightenment; and the loving-kindness of awakening is through the state of equal flavor.
The love that is free from superimposition, by virtue of abandoning attachment and aversion; the love of great compassion, by virtue of illuminating the Mahāyāna;
and the love that is free from weariness, by virtue of contemplating emptiness and selflessness.
The loving-kindness of the gift of Dharma through the absence of a teacher’s closed fist; the loving-kindness of ethical discipline through regard for beings of immoral conduct;
the loving-kindness of patience through not harming oneself or others.
The loving-kindness of vigor consists in bearing the burden of all sentient beings; the loving-kindness of meditative concentration consists in being free from relishing;
the loving-kindness of wisdom consists in bringing [beings] to the appropriate time.
Skillful means-love through showing the way in all directions;
honesty-love through the purity of intention; and lack of deceit-love through sincerity of intention.
The loving-kindness of resolute intention is due to being free from afflictions; the loving-kindness of non-deceit is due to being uncontrived;
the loving-kindness of happiness is due to establishing others in the happiness of a Buddha.
"This, Mañjuśrī, is the great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*) of a bodhisattva.
He asked: "What, then, is his great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)?
He replied: "It is that one relinquishes every root of merit (*kuśalamūla*) as it is performed, for the sake of all sentient beings."
He asked: "What, then, is his great sympathetic joy?
He replied: "That which, having given, one becomes glad and does not feel regret."
He asked: "What, then, is his great equanimity?
He replied: "It is the state of being purposeful in both respects.
He asked: "By one who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, what should be practiced?"
He said: "Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva who is terrified by the fear of saṃsāra should practice the majesty of the Buddha.
He asked: "One who wishes to abide in the majesty of the Buddha, where should they abide?
He replied: "One who wishes to abide in the majesty of the Buddha should abide in the equality of all sentient beings."
He asked: "By one who wishes to abide in the equality of all sentient beings, where should they abide?

He replied: "By one who wishes to abide in the equality of all sentient beings, they should abide for the sake of the liberation of all sentient beings. He asked: "By one who wishes to effect the liberation of all sentient beings, what should be done?"
He said: "One who wishes to effect the liberation of all sentient beings must effect the liberation from the afflictions (*kleśa*).
He asked: "By one who wishes to cast off the afflictions, how should one apply oneself?
He replied: "By one who wishes to cast off the afflictions, one should apply oneself through proper fundamental method (*yoniśas*)."

He asked: "Furthermore, how is one who is engaged [in practice] rightly engaged? He replied: "One who is engaged in non-arising and non-cessation is rightly engaged. He asked: "What does he not produce?"
What does he not cease?
He said: He does not give rise to the unwholesome, and he does not cease the wholesome.
He asked: "What is the root of the wholesome and the unwholesome?
He replied: "The view of a self-entity (satkāya) is the root.
He asked again: "And what, in turn, is the root of the view of a self-entity?"
He said: "The root of the view of a self-identity (satkāya) is desire and greed. He asked: "What is the root of desire and greed?
He replied: "The root of desire and greed is unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa)."
He asked: "What is the root of unreal imagination?
He replied: "The root of unreal imagination is perverted perception.
He asked: "What is the root of perverted perception?"
He said: "The root of perverted perception is non-abiding.
He asked: "What is the root of non-abiding?
He replied: "Mañjuśrī, as for that which is non-abiding, what could possibly be its root?"
Thus, indeed, all phenomena are established upon the root of non-establishment.
Then, the deity who resided in that house,
having heard this teaching on the Dharma from those bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, was satisfied, uplifted, and joyful in mind.
Manifesting a gross physical form, he scattered divine flowers over those great beings and those great śrāvakas.
Of those who were thus strewn with flowers, the flowers that fell upon the bodies of the bodhisattvas remained fixed upon the surface of the earth.
Furthermore, as for the flowers that fell upon the bodies of the great śrāvakas, they remained right there and did not fall to the ground;
then those great śrāvakas cast off those flowers by means of their miraculous powers.
And yet they do not fall.
Then that deity said this to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, what [is this]?"
“You are casting away these flowers.
She said: “O deity, these flowers are unfit;
therefore, I am removing these flowers.”
The deity said: "Venerable Śāriputra, do not speak thus.
For what reason?
Because these flowers are pure."
What is the reason?
It is because these flowers do not conceptualize nor discriminate,
whereas the Elder Śāriputra, on the other hand, does conceptualize and discriminate.
Venerable Śāriputra, those who conceptualize and discriminate regarding the going forth in the well-expounded Dharma and Vinaya are improper;
yet the Elder himself conceptualizes and discriminates.
But those who do not conceptualize and do not discriminate— they are the ones who conceptualize!
Look, Venerable Śāriputra, how the flowers do not adhere to the bodies of these great beings.
Just as, for instance, because all conceptual constructions and discursive thoughts have been abandoned,
non-human spirits find no opportunity to gain entry against a person of timid nature;
even so, for those who are terrified by the fear of saṃsāra, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles find no opportunity to gain entry.
Furthermore, for those who have become free from the fear of all the afflictions of saṃsāra,
what can forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles do to them? For them, the latent predispositions have been abandoned.
Flowers adhere to their bodies;
therefore, flowers do not adhere to the bodies of those who have abandoned all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Then, the venerable Śāriputra said this to that goddess:
"But for how long have you been established here in this house, O goddess?
She replied: "As long as the noble liberation of the Elder has been established.
He said: "You have not been established here in this house for long, O goddess."
He asked: "How long has the Venerable One’s noble liberation been established? Thereupon, the Elder remained silent.
He said: "Why now has the Elder, the foremost among those of great wisdom, remained silent?"
He did not answer the question when the time for it had come.
He said: "O goddess, liberation is indeed beyond verbal expression;
therefore, I do not know what I should say."
He said: Whatever syllable the Elder utters, all these syllables have liberation as their characteristic. For what reason?
For that which is liberation is not apprehended internally, nor externally, nor in between the two;
likewise, so too are syllables.
Therefore, Reverend Śāriputra, do not point out liberation by means of the removal of syllables. For what reason?
Because liberation is indeed the sameness of all phenomena.
He said: "But, O goddess, is it not the case that liberation is the departure from passion, hatred, and delusion?
The goddess replied: "This teaching—that liberation is the departure from passion, hatred, and delusion—is for those who possess conceit.
As for those who are free from conceit,"
For them, the very nature of passion, hatred, and delusion is liberation.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra said this to that goddess:
"Excellent, excellent, goddess! What have you attained, or what have you realized?"
"Such is her inspired eloquence.
He said: "Venerable Śāriputra, I have not attained or realized anything; that is why I possess such inspired eloquence."
Those who think, "We have attained this" or "We have realized this," are said to be conceited regarding the well-proclaimed Dharma and Vinaya.
[Vimalakīrti] asked: "Goddess, are you a follower of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, or the Mahāyāna?"

He said: "I belong to the vehicle of the disciples by way of indicating the Śrāvaka-yāna; I belong to the vehicle of the solitary buddhas by way of entering the dharma of dependent origination; I belong to the Great Vehicle by way of not relinquishing great compassion."
Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, those who have entered a grove of *campaka* trees do not smell the scent of the castor-oil plant (*eraṇḍa*);
rather, having entered a grove of *campaka* trees, they smell only the scent of the *campaka*.
In the same way, Reverend Śāriputra, those dwelling here in this house, which is fragrant with the virtues of the Buddha-dharma, do not smell the scents of the disciples or the solitary buddhas.

Venerable Śāriputra, even those Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, and mahoragas who enter this house depart having generated the mind of awakening through hearing the Dharma from this noble person and by means of the fragrance of the qualities of the Buddha-dharma.
Venerable Śāriputra, during my twelve years of residence here, I have never before heard a discourse associated with the disciples or the solitary buddhas.
It is associated exclusively with great loving-kindness and great compassion, and exclusively with inconceivable phenomena.
"Venerable Śāriputra, in this house eight wonderful and marvelous qualities are constantly and perpetually manifest. What are these eight?"
Here neither night nor day is discerned; this house is perpetually illuminated by a golden-colored radiance.
Here neither the sun nor the moon is discerned, nor do they shine.
This is the first marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, for those who enter this house, as soon as they have entered, none of their afflictions cause them any distress.
This is the second marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, this house is never devoid of Śakra, Brahmā, the world-protectors, and bodhisattvas who have gathered from other buddha-fields.
This is the third marvelous and extraordinary quality.

Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, this house is constantly and perpetually never devoid of the hearing of the Dharma, of discourse connected with the six perfections, and of irreversible teachings on the Dharma; this is the fourth marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, Reverend Śāriputra, whatever musical performances or divine and human instruments are played here in this house,
From those musical instruments, an immeasurable production of the sound of the Dharma issues forth at all times.
This is the fifth marvelous and wonderful quality.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, in this house there are four great treasuries, filled with all kinds of jewels and inexhaustible, from which all the poor and wretched take their fill and depart.
And they do not diminish;
this is the sixth marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, here in this house dwell the Tathāgatas Śākyamuni, Amitābha, Akṣobhya, and Ratnaśrī.

Ratnārci, Ratnacandra, Ratnavyūha, Duḥprasaha, Sarvārthasiddha, Prabhūtaratna, Siṃhanādanādin, and Siṃhaghoṣa Tathāgata— these and immeasurable other Tathāgatas in the ten directions, headed by these, come at the mere thought of this noble being.
Having arrived, they teach the entrance into the Dharma-door called "The Secret of the Tathāgata" and then depart.
This is the seventh marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Furthermore, Venerable Śāriputra, within this house all the arrays of the abodes of the gods and all the arrays of the qualities of the Buddha-fields are visible.
This is the eighth marvelous and extraordinary quality.
Venerable Śāriputra, these eight marvelous and extraordinary qualities are constantly and perpetually seen here in this house.
For what reason?
"Who, seeing this inconceivable nature of phenomena, would long for the nature of a śrāvaka?
He asked: "Goddess, why do you not transform away your female state?
She replied: "For twelve full years now, I have been searching for my female state, yet I have not found it."
Moreover, Reverend Śāriputra, suppose a woman were created by a magician, and someone were to say to her:
"Why do you not transform out of this female state?
What would she say?
He said: "There is no real, perfected existence of it.
He said: "In the same way, Reverend Śāriputra, since all phenomena are unperfected and have the nature of magical illusions, how can you think thus:
'Why do you not transform away this female state?'"
Then that deity exercised such a supernatural power (*adhiṣṭhāna*) that the Elder Śāriputra appeared exactly as that deity was,
and that deity appeared exactly as the Elder was.
Then that deity, appearing in the form of Śāriputra, asked Śāriputra— who was himself wearing the form of a deity—
“Venerable Śāriputra, why do you not transform away this female state?
Śāriputra, in his form as a deity, replied:
"I do not know what I should turn back from.
My male form disappeared and a female form manifested for me.
She said: "If the Elder is able to turn back this female state,"
Then all women, too, will turn back from their female state;
just as the Elder is not a woman yet appears like one, so too for all women, their female form will cease to exist, and they will no longer appear as women with female forms.
With this in mind, the Blessed One said:
"All phenomena are neither female nor male.
Then that deity withdrew that supernatural manifestation.
Then the Venerable Śāriputra once again became endowed with his own original form.
Then that goddess said this to the Venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, where has your female form gone?"
He said: "It is neither made nor transformed.
He said: "In this very way, all phenomena (dharmas) are neither made nor transformed. That wherein there is neither making nor transformation—that is the word of the Buddha."
He asked: "Goddess, having passed away from here, where will you be reborn?
She replied: "I shall be reborn wherever a transformation of the Tathāgata is reborn."
He said: "For one emanated by a Tathāgata, there is neither death nor rebirth.
He said: "In the very same way, for all phenomena, there is neither death nor rebirth.
He asked: "Furthermore, O Goddess, after how long will you fully awaken to enlightenment?"
He said: "When the Elder shall be endowed with the qualities of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), then I shall fully awaken to enlightenment.
She said: "O Goddess, it is impossible that I should be endowed with the qualities of an ordinary person."
He said: "In just this way, Reverend Śāriputra, it is impossible that I shall fully awaken to enlightenment.
Why is that?
For enlightenment is established precisely in the absence of a fixed location."
"Therefore, it is impossible that anyone will attain perfect awakening.
The Elder said:
"O Goddess, the Tathāgata has stated: 'Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges have attained perfect awakening, are attaining perfect awakening, and will attain perfect awakening.'"
The deity said: "Venerable Śāriputra, this is merely a conventional designation for the enumeration of syllables, namely 'the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
Yet, there are no Buddhas that are past, future, or present;
for awakening transcends the three times."
Moreover, the Elder has attained Arhatship. He said: "It is attained by means of non-attainment. He said: "In this very way, perfect awakening is [attained] by means of non-awakening."
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said to the venerable Śāriputra:

"Venerable Śāriputra, this goddess has served ninety-two billion buddhas; she sports with the knowledge of supernormal powers, is established in her vows, has attained patient acceptance, and has entered the stage of non-retrogression. By the power of her vows, she remains here in whatever manner she desires."
For the sake of maturing sentient beings.
The sixth chapter: The Chapter on the Deities.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
“Noble son, how does a bodhisattva become one who has reached the further shore in the Buddha-dharmas? He replied: “Mañjuśrī, it is when a bodhisattva goes by way of non-going.”
At that time, the bodhisattva has reached the ultimate goal regarding the qualities of a Buddha.
He asked: "What is the bodhisattva’s going where one should not go?
He replied: "When he goes even to the state of the five deeds of immediate retribution..."
He does not become corrupted by ill-will or harmfulness,
yet he goes to the realm of hell,
and he becomes free from all dust and afflictions.
He goes to the realm of animals,
yet he is free from the darkness of ignorance;
he goes to the realm of asuras, yet...
He becomes free from pride, intoxication, and arrogance;
yet he goes to the realm of Yama,
while having accumulated all the provisions of merit and wisdom.
He goes to the state of immovable form, yet he does not become one who has entered into that state;
he goes to the state of passion, yet...
He becomes free from passion for all sensual enjoyments;
he enters the path of faultlessness and remains unimpeded toward all sentient beings.
He follows the course of delusion,
yet his mind remains focused on wisdom regarding all phenomena;
he follows the course of stinginess, yet...
He becomes one who renounces all internal and external things, regardless of body or life;
he enters the path of those with immoral conduct,
yet remains established in all moral precepts, trainings, ascetic virtues, and self-effacement, perceiving danger even in the slightest faults.
He may follow the course of malice, stubbornness, and anger,
yet he dwells in loving-kindness with a mind that is utterly free from ill-will; he may follow the course of indolence, yet...

He is devoted to the pursuit of all roots of virtue and exerts effort with unremitting vigor; he follows the course of unconfused faculties and, being naturally absorbed in meditative concentration, his dhyāna is never empty.
He follows the course of faulty wisdom,
yet he becomes skilled in all mundane and supramundane treatises, having reached the consummation of the perfection of wisdom;
he follows the course of hypocrisy and flattery.
He has emerged from the practice of skillful means and is proficient in intentional language;
he displays the ways of pride,
yet he serves as a bridge and a causeway for the entire world.
He enters the course of the afflictions,
yet he is naturally pure and utterly undefiled; he enters the course of Māra, yet...
He becomes independent of others regarding all the qualities of a Buddha;
he follows the path of the śrāvakas,
yet he causes sentient beings to hear the Dharma they have never heard before.
He goes to the way of the pratyekabuddhas,
yet he is motivated by great compassion for the sake of maturing sentient beings;
he goes to the way of the poor, yet...
He has attained the state of having jewel-like hands and possesses inexhaustible enjoyments;
yet he also goes to the realm of those with impaired faculties.
He is adorned with the primary marks and is handsome;
yet he takes birth in a lowly family,
while being born into the lineage and clan of the Tathāgatas, having accumulated the provisions of merit and wisdom.
He undergoes the state of being weak, ill-favored, and dejected, yet he possesses a body like that of Nārāyaṇa and is pleasing to behold for all sentient beings;
he displays the conduct of one who is aged, diseased, and infirm.
He has utterly eradicated all illness and has transcended the fear of death;
he displays the course of worldly enjoyments,
yet he is frequently contemplative of the perception of impermanence and has brought all seeking to rest.
The Bodhisattva displays the array of the inner apartments and theatrical performances,
yet he has crossed over the mire of sensual desires and wanders without a fixed abode;
he even adopts the manner of those with dull faculties.
He becomes adorned with manifold eloquence and has attained the dhāraṇīs;
he enters the way of the non-Buddhist teachers and becomes like one of those teachers.
He goes along the course of all worlds,
yet he is turned away from all courses;
he goes along the course of nirvāṇa.
And yet, he does not abandon the continuity of saṃsāra.
In this way, Mañjuśrī, a bodhisattva goes by way of non-going, and having gone, he has reached all the qualities of a Buddha.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said this to the crown prince Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī, what is the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgatas?
He replied: “Noble son, the view of a self-identity (*satkāya*) is the lineage of the Tathāgatas.”
Ignorance and craving for existence are the lineage;
passion, hatred, and delusion are the lineage;
the four perversions are the lineage.
The five hindrances are the lineage; the six sense bases are the lineage;
the seven stations of consciousness are the lineage.
The eight types of wrong views are the lineage; the nine bases of malice are the lineage;
the ten unwholesome paths of action are the lineage.
"Noble son, this is the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
In brief, noble son, the sixty-two types of views are the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
Mañjuśrī was asked: "With what intention do you speak thus?"
He said: "Noble son, it is not possible for one who has seen the unconditioned and is established in the path of certainty (niyāma) to generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
It is possible for one who dwells within the conditioned house of the afflictions and has not yet seen the truths to generate the mind set on unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Noble son, it is just as, for example, blue, red, white, and fragrant lotuses do not grow in dry upland soils."
Blue lotuses, red lotuses, night-blooming water lilies, white lotuses, and fragrant saugandhika flowers grow when cast upon the mud and sandbanks;
in just the same way, noble son, the qualities of a Buddha do not grow among sentient beings who have reached the fixed determination of the unconditioned,
but the qualities of a Buddha grow among sentient beings who have fallen into the mud and sandbanks of the afflictions.
Just as, for example, seeds do not grow in the sky,
but grow when established upon the surface of the earth;
even so, the qualities of a Buddha do not grow in those who have attained the fixed determination of the unconditioned.
Having generated a view of a self-existent body as vast as Mount Sumeru, the thought of awakening arises;
from that, the qualities of a Buddha grow.
Therefore, noble son, by this method also, it should be understood in this way.
In whatever way all afflictions exist, in that very way is the lineage (*gotra*) of the Tathāgatas.
For example, noble son, just as it is impossible to extract a priceless jewel without having entered the great ocean,
even so, it is impossible for one who has not entered the ocean of afflictions to give rise to the jewel of the mind of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-citta*).
Then the Elder Mahākāśyapa gave his approval to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, Mañjuśrī! These words you have spoken are well-spoken and true. These afflictions are the lineage of the Tathāgatas."
For how could those like us have the power to generate the thought of awakening right now?
One who has committed the five deeds of immediate retribution is capable of generating the thought of awakening;
such a person is capable of fully awakening to the qualities of a Buddha.
Furthermore,
Vkn, just as the five strands of sensual pleasure are devoid of quality and ineffective for a man with impaired faculties,
even so, all the qualities of a Buddha are devoid of quality and ineffective for a śrāvaka who has abandoned all fetters.
He no longer has the power to take them as objects of his attachment;
therefore, Mañjuśrī, ordinary worldlings are grateful to the Tathāgata,
but the śrāvakas are not.
For what reason?
Because ordinary persons, upon hearing of the qualities of a Buddha, generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment so that the lineage of the Three Jewels may not be interrupted;
whereas disciples, even though they hear of the Buddha's dharmas, powers, and intrepidities for as long as they live, are not capable of generating the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.
Then, a bodhisattva named Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana, who was present and seated in that very assembly,
spoke thus to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"Householder, where are your mother and father, your female and male slaves, your laborers, and your servants?"
"Where are friends, kinsmen, and blood relations? Where is one's retinue, or the vehicles of horses, elephants, chariots, and infantry?
When this was said, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana with these verses:
O worthy one, the Perfection of Wisdom is the mother of the Bodhisattvas,
and Skillful Means is their father, from whom the Leaders are born.
The Dharma-delight is their wife, and Loving-kindness and Compassion are their two daughters.
Truth and Dharma are both sons; the contemplation of the meaning of emptiness is the home.
All afflictions are likewise disciples, obedient to his will as he desires.
The factors of enlightenment are his friends, by means of which he awakens to supreme enlightenment.
These six perfections are indeed their constant companions;
the means of attraction are their harem, and the teachings are their songs and music. Their park is the dhāraṇīs, strewn with the flowers of the factors of enlightenment.
The fruit is the knowledge of liberation, and the trees are the great wealth of the Dharma.
(5) The lotus ponds are the liberations, filled with the nets of meditative concentrations;
covered with the lotuses of purity, therein the stainless ones bathe. (6)
The superknowledges are their vehicle, the unsurpassed Mahāyāna;
the mind of awakening is the charioteer, while the auspicious eightfold path is the way.
Their ornaments are the primary marks and the eighty secondary characteristics. (7)
Clad in the garments of shame and modesty, they possess virtuous intentions and are auspicious.
(8) They possess the wealth of the True Dharma; their application is the teaching of the Dharma, their practice is the great gain, and their dedication is toward awakening. (9)

The four meditative absorptions (dhyānas), spread out with pure livelihood, are their bed; wisdom, constantly composed through hearing [the Dharma], is their awakening. Immortality is their food, and the essence of liberation is their drink. (10)
Purity of intention is their bath; ethical discipline is their fragrant ointment.
Because they have utterly destroyed the enemy of the afflictions, they are heroes indeed, unconquered.
Taking up residence at the banner of the seat of awakening, they subdue the four Māras.
Intentionally manifesting birth, though they are unborn and without origin,
they appear in all fields like the rising of the king of rays.
Having honored millions of Buddhas, the Leaders, with every kind of offering, they [attain this state].
They never form any attachment to a self or to a buddha.
They purify buddha-fields according to the conduct of sentient beings; having reached the realm of space, they have no perception of a "sentient being" regarding sentient beings. (14–15)
In a single instant, the confident Bodhisattvas manifest all the forms, sounds, and utterances produced by all sentient beings;
they recognize the deeds of Māra, yet they also follow along with those who act as Māras. (16)
Having attained the perfection of skillful means, they display every kind of activity.
(17) They appear as aged, diseased, or even show themselves as dead; dwelling in the nature of illusion, they do this for the sake of maturing sentient beings. (18)
They display the conflagration at the end of an eon, burning that very earth,
in order to show the impermanence to beings who perceive things as permanent.
(19) Invited by thousands of millions of beings within a single kingdom, they accept the offerings.
They eat at the homes of all and lead everyone toward awakening.
Whatever mantra-knowledges or various kinds of arts and crafts there may be, they have attained mastery in them all and bring happiness to all sentient beings. (20–21)
However many heretics there are in the world, they go forth everywhere;
indeed, they liberate sentient beings who have fallen into various types of wrong views.
They become moons or suns, Śakras, Brahmās, or lords of progeny.
They become water, fire, earth, and likewise wind.
During the intermediate kalpas of disease, they become the supreme medicine by which sentient beings are liberated, becoming happy and free from illness. (23–24)
During the intermediate kalpas of famine, they become food and drink;
having removed hunger and thirst, they teach the Dharma to living beings.
During the intermediate kalpas of weapons, they become practitioners of loving-kindness.
They lead many hundreds of millions of beings toward non-malice.
And in the midst of great battles, those Bodhisattvas of great power remain impartial; they delight in reconciliation and harmony. (26–27)
And whatever inconceivable hells there may be within the buddha-fields,
they intentionally go there for the sake of benefiting sentient beings. (28) Whatever realms of existence are manifested within the animal womb, [they enter them all].
They teach the Dharma everywhere; therefore they are called leaders.
They display the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, yet they also display meditative absorption to those who practice meditation.
They render Māra helpless and allow him no opportunity for entry.
Just as one might display a lotus in the midst of fire as a marvel,
so too will you display both sensual pleasures and meditative concentration as a marvel.
Having reflected, they become courtesans for the sake of attracting men.
Having enticed them with the goad of passion, they establish them in the wisdom of a Buddha.
(32) For the sake of benefiting sentient beings, they always become village headmen, caravan leaders, and domestic priests; they become chief ministers and ministers as well. (33)
They become an inexhaustible treasury for sentient beings who are poor,
for by giving gifts to them, those beings generate the mind of awakening.
Toward sentient beings stiffened by pride, they become great champions.
They pray for supreme enlightenment, which uproots all mental afflictions.
They always stand before sentient beings who are oppressed by fear;
having granted them fearlessness, they bring them to maturity for the sake of enlightenment. (35–36)
Having become seers possessing the five superknowledges and living as celibate practitioners,
they enjoin sentient beings toward ethical discipline, patience, gentleness, and self-restraint.
Here, the Leaders perceive sentient beings who are heavy with the burden of service.
They become servants or slaves, and they even enter into the state of discipleship.
Whichever limb [of existence] sentient beings might delight in through the Dharma, those well-trained in the great skillful means manifest all such activities. (38–39)
For their training is indeed infinite, and their sphere of activity is also infinite;
they are endowed with infinite wisdom and are liberators of infinite living beings.
Even in ten million eons, or even in hundreds of millions of eons, [one could not exhaustively describe them].
Even if all the Buddhas were to speak, they could not reach the end of its qualities; it is truly beyond words.
(41) Having heard these teachings, what wise person would not aspire to supreme enlightenment, except for those of inferior nature who possess no wisdom? (42)
Thus it is said.
The seventh chapter: The Lineage of the Tathāgata.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed those bodhisattvas:
"May the noble sons be inspired to speak: what is the entrance into the non-dual dharma-door of the bodhisattvas?
At that time, a bodhisattva named Dharmavikurvaṇa was present in the assembly.
He spoke thus: "Noble son, arising and ceasing are a duality.
That which is neither born nor arisen has no cessation whatsoever. The attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena is the entrance into non-duality."
The bodhisattva Śrīgupta said:
"‘I’ and ‘mine’—these two are a duality.
Through the non-superimposition of a self, the notion of ‘mine’ does not arise."
And this non-superimposition is the entrance into nonduality.
The bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa said:
"‘Affliction’ and ‘purification’—these two are dualistic."
Through the thorough knowledge of affliction (*saṃkleśa*), there is no conceiving of purification (*vyavadāna*).
The path leading to the state of conformity, which is the total eradication of all conceiving—this is the entrance into non-duality.
Sunakṣatra, the bodhisattva, said:
"Vibration" and "mental engagement"—these two are a duality.
That which, moreover, neither vibrates nor engages the mind is without objective domain; being devoid of an objective domain, this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Subāhu said:
"The thought of awakening and the thought of a disciple—these two are a duality.
However, that which is the perception of the thought of awakening as being equal to an illusory mind—in that, there is neither the thought of awakening nor the thought of a disciple."
That which is the state of the mind having identical characteristics—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Animiṣa said:
"Appropriation and non-appropriation—these two are a duality."
That which one does not grasp, one does not apprehend;
therein, one performs neither affirmation nor negation.
This non-activity and non-involvement with all phenomena is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Sunetra said:
"‘Single characteristic’ and ‘characteristicless’—these two are a duality.
That which, moreover, does not characterize and does not conceptualize,"
He does not make it have a single characteristic, nor does he make it characterless.
This entry into the equality of characteristics and the distinction from characteristics is the entry into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Puṣya said:
The wholesome and the unwholesome—these two are a duality.
That which is the non-apprehension of the wholesome and the unwholesome is the signless.
And the non-duality of the limit of the signless is suchness.
Where there is the state of having reached the further shore, that is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Siṃha said:
"Faultiness and faultlessness—these two are a duality."
Furthermore, because knowledge is firmly bound by the vajra, one is neither bound nor liberated; this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Siṃhamati said:
"To say 'this is with outflows' and 'this is without outflows'—this is duality."

Furthermore, one who has attained the equality of dharmas does not form the notion of "with outflows" or "without outflows," nor is he one who has attained non-perception, nor is he one who has attained equality within the equality of non-perception.
He is not bound by perceptions.
Such an entry as this is the entry into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Sukhādhimukta said:
"This is pleasure" and "this is pain"—these are two.
However, when one is free from all pleasure and possesses a mind equal to space, not forming perceptions due to the utter purity of knowledge, this is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Nārāyaṇa said:
"This is mundane" and "this is supramundane"—these are two.
That which is the natural emptiness of the mundane is not something from which one emerges, nor into which one enters; it is not driven forward, nor does it disperse.
Where there is no crossing over, no descending, no going forth, and no dispersing—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Dāntamati said:
"‘Saṃsāra’ and ‘nirvāṇa’—these two are a duality."
By seeing the intrinsic nature of saṃsāra, one neither transmigrates nor enters final nirvāṇa. Such an awakening is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Pratyakṣadarśin said:
"Exhaustion" and "non-exhaustion"—these two are a duality.
Exhaustion is absolute exhaustion;
and that which is absolutely exhausted is not something to be further exhausted.
Therefore it is called "inexhaustible.
That which is inexhaustible is momentary;
for that which is momentary, there is no exhaustion.
One who has entered in this way should be said to have entered the gateway of the non-dual Dharma.
The Bodhisattva Samantagupta said:
"‘Self’ and ‘selflessness’—these two are a duality."
He who does not perceive that selfhood—how could he make anything "selfless"?
One who perceives the intrinsic nature of the self does not construct duality; this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Vidyuddeva said:
"Knowledge and ignorance—these two are a duality.
Knowledge has ignorance as its very nature."
That which is ignorance is without intrinsic nature, beyond calculation, and transcends the path of reckoning.
The realization of this is non-dual realization; this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Priyadarśana said:
"Form is empty"—these two are a duality.
For form itself is emptiness;
emptiness does not arise from the destruction of form.
The very nature of form is emptiness;
likewise, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty—these two are a duality.
For consciousness itself is indeed emptiness.
Emptiness does not arise from the destruction of consciousness;
rather, the very nature of consciousness is emptiness.
That realization and awakening regarding these five aggregates of clinging in this manner is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Prabhāketu said:
"To say that the four elements are one thing and the space element is another—this is duality.
The four elements have the very nature of space."

From the perspective of the past, they have the nature of space; from the perspective of the future, they have the nature of space; likewise, from the perspective of the present, they also have the nature of space.
This knowledge of entering into the realms in such a manner is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Sumati said:
The eye and form—these two constitute a duality.
However, one who has fully understood the eye does not become attached to forms, does not feel aversion toward them, and is not deluded by them; such a person is said to be "peaceful."
The ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, the body and tangibles, and the mind and mental phenomena—this is duality.
However, one who has fully understood the mind does not become attached to, does not feel aversion toward, and is not deluded by mental phenomena; such a person is said to be "peaceful."
In this way, for one who abides in peace, there is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamati said:
"To dedicate generosity toward omniscience—this is duality."
The nature of giving is itself omniscience, and the nature of omniscience is itself the dedication [of merit].
Likewise, to dedicate ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom toward omniscience— these two are one.
Omniscience has wisdom as its very nature,
and transformation has omniscience as its very nature. This entry into the single principle herein is the entry into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Gambhīrabuddhi said:
"To say that emptiness is one thing, the signless another, and the wishless another—this is duality.
For that which is empty contains no sign whatsoever."
In the signless there is the wishless;
in the wishless, neither mind, nor intellect, nor mental consciousness functions.
Where there is one gate of liberation, all gates of liberation are to be seen therein—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Śāntendriya said:
"‘Buddha,’ ‘Dharma,’ and ‘Saṅgha’—these are a duality.
For the Dharma belongs to the Buddha."
The Saṅgha has the nature of the Dharma;
all these jewels are unconditioned,
and space is also unconditioned.
The principle of all phenomena is equal to space;
this very realization is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Apratihatacaksus said:
"The body of existence" and "the cessation of the body of existence"—these are two.
For the body of existence itself is indeed cessation.
Why is that?
For he does not give rise to the view that "this is a self-existent body" (satkāya),
by means of which view one would conceptualize either a "self-existent body" or the "cessation of the self-existent body.
He is without conceptualization, free from conceptualization, and utterly beyond conceptualization, having attained the nature of cessation.
"It neither comes into being nor passes away; this is the entrance into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Suvinīta said:
"To speak of 'restraint of body, speech, and mind' is duality."
For what reason?
Because these phenomena have the characteristic of being unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Whatever is the unconditioned nature of the body, that is precisely the characteristic of the unconditioned nature of speech; that is precisely the characteristic of the unconditioned nature of the mind.
That which is the non-constructive nature of all phenomena is to be known and followed;
that knowledge of non-constructiveness herein is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Puṇyakṣetra said:
"To form meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable volitional formations—this is duality.
However, that which is the non-formation of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable [volitional formations] is non-dual."

That which is the emptiness of the specific characteristics of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations—therein, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formations do not exist.
This kind of thorough investigation is the entrance into non-duality.
Thus spoke the bodhisattva Padmavyūha.
The duality arises from the arising of the self;
one who has fully understood the self does not give rise to this duality.
For one who abides in non-duality, there is no representation.
And the entrance into non-duality is without informative intimation.
The bodhisattva Śrīgarbha said:
"Duality is characterized by objective apprehension."
What one does not obtain, one does not apprehend; that one neither accumulates nor discards.
In this, there is neither accumulation nor discarding—this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Candrottara said:
"Darkness and light—these two are a duality.
That which is neither darkness nor light is non-duality."
For what reason?
Because for one who has entered the attainment of cessation, there is neither darkness nor light;
and all phenomena have such characteristics.
"The entry into equality herein is the entry into non-duality.
The Bodhisattva Ratnamudrāhasta said:
"To delight in nirvana and to not delight in samsara—this is duality."
That which has no delight in nirvāṇa and no lack of delight in saṃsāra—this is non-duality. For what reason?
Because liberation is proclaimed only for one who is bound.
"One who is fundamentally unbound—how could such a person seek liberation?
A monk who is neither bound nor liberated gives rise to neither attachment nor aversion; this is the entrance into non-duality.
Thus spoke the Bodhisattva Maṇikūṭarāja.
"The path" and "the wrong path"—these are two.
For one who has entered the path, the wrong path does not manifest.
For one who abides in its non-manifestation, there is neither the perception of a path nor the perception of a wrong path.
For one who has fully understood perceptions, the intellect does not enter into duality; this is the entrance into non-duality.
The bodhisattva Satyanandin said:
"‘Truth’ and ‘falsehood’—this is duality."
One who sees the truth does not perceive even truth;
how then could they see falsehood?
For what reason?
For he does not see with the fleshly eye;
he sees with the eye of wisdom,
and he sees in such a manner.
One does not discern. Where there is neither seeing nor discerning, this is the entrance into non-duality.
(Vkn 8.32) Having thus each explained their own teachings, those bodhisattvas said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, what is the bodhisattva’s entrance into non-duality? Mañjuśrī replied, "O noble sons, everything you have all said is well-spoken."
"Moreover, all that you have pointed out is duality.

Setting aside this single teaching—that which is the non-utterance, the non-proclamation, the non-issuing, the non-recitation, the non-expression, and the non-designation of all phenomena—this is the entrance into non-duality.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"Noble son, we have each given our own exposition. May you also now provide an exposition on the entrance into the non-dual Dharma.
Thereupon, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti remained silent.
Then Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta gave his approval to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, saying:
"Excellent, excellent, noble son! This is the entrance into the non-dual dharma-gate of the bodhisattvas, wherein there is no movement of syllables, sounds, cries, or conceptualizations.

While this teaching was being expounded, five thousand bodhisattvas, through their entry into the non-dual dharma-gate, attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The eighth chapter: Entering the Dharma-Door of Non-Duality.
Then, this thought occurred to the venerable Śāriputra: "The time has come to its end,
yet these great beings do not rise."
"Where will these be consumed?
Then, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, knowing with his own mind the reflection in the mind of the venerable Śāriputra, said to the venerable Śāriputra:
"Venerable Śāriputra, dwell in those eight liberations which have been taught by the Tathāgata."
"Do not listen to the Dharma with a mental continuum smeared by worldly gain;
rather, Reverend Śāriputra, wait for a moment until you shall eat food such as has never been tasted before."

Then, at that time, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti entered such a state of meditative concentration and performed such a miraculous feat that he manifested to those bodhisattvas and great śrāvakas the world-system named Sarvagandhasugandhā, located in the upward direction beyond as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges rivers, past this very buddha-field.
There, the Tathāgata named Gandhottamakūṭa currently resides, stays, and maintains his life.
And in that world-system, whatever divine and human fragrances waft through all the buddha-fields in the ten directions,
those most excellent fragrances waft from the trees in that world-system.
In that world-system, even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist;
there is only an assembly of pure bodhisattvas.
To them, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa teaches the Dharma.
And in that world-system, the gabled halls are composed entirely of all kinds of perfumes, as are the walkways, gardens, and celestial palaces.
Furthermore, the fragrance of the food which those bodhisattvas consume pervades immeasurable world-systems.
And at that time, the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa, was seated for his meal together with those bodhisattvas.
There, the sons of gods named Gandhavyūhāhāra, who had set out in the Mahāyāna, were intent upon attending to and serving that Blessed One and those bodhisattvas.
Then the entire assembly saw that world-system, and they saw that Blessed One and those bodhisattvas seated at the head of the meal.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed all those bodhisattvas:
"O noble sirs, who among you is able to bring food from that buddha-field?
Due to Mañjuśrī’s spiritual power, no one ventured to do so.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said this to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta:
"Mañjuśrī, are you not ashamed of such an assembly?
He replied: "Noble son, has it not been said by the Tathāgata that one who is untrained should not be despised?"
Then, without rising from his bed, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti manifested before those bodhisattvas an emanated bodhisattva.
With a body the color of gold, adorned with the primary and secondary marks, his radiance was such that the entire assembly was eclipsed by it.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti spoke thus to that emanated bodhisattva:
Go, noble son, toward the upward direction; after passing through as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges rivers, there is a world-system named Sarvagandhasugandhā.
There dwells a Tathāgata named Gandhottamakūṭa, who is currently seated for his meal.

Having gone there, prostrate with your head at the feet of that Tathāgata in my name and say this: "The Licchavi Vimalakīrti, having prostrated with his head at the Blessed One's feet, inquires after the Blessed One’s freedom from illness, freedom from affliction, physical lightness, ease of movement, strength, well-being, blamelessness, and state of comfort."
And he spoke thus: "O Blessed One, give me the remains of your meal, which shall perform the work of a Buddha in the Sahā world-system;
it shall cause these beings of inferior inclinations to find delight in a noble resolve, and the name of the Tathāgata shall be made widely known."
Then that emanated bodhisattva, having replied "Very well" to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, appeared with his face turned upward before those bodhisattvas;
yet those bodhisattvas did not see him as he departed.
Then that emanated bodhisattva arrived at that world-system called Sarvagandhasugandhā.

There, having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa, he spoke thus: "Blessed One, the bodhisattva Vimalakīrti bows his head at the feet of the Blessed One; he inquires after your freedom from illness, your freedom from affliction, your lightness of movement, your well-being, your strength, your happiness, your blamelessness, and your state of comfort."
Having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, he spoke thus:

"Blessed One, give me the remains of your meal; it will perform the work of a Buddha in this Sahā world-system, causing those beings of inferior inclinations to take delight in their minds toward the sublime qualities of a Buddha."
And the name of the Blessed One will become widely renowned.
Then, indeed, those bodhisattvas in the buddha-field of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa, were struck with wonder and said this to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa:
“From where, Blessed One, does such a great being as this come?
Where is that Sahā world-system?
What is this so-called ‘inclination toward the inferior’?”
Thus those bodhisattvas questioned that Tathāgata.
Then the Blessed One said to those bodhisattvas:
"Noble sons, in the downward direction from this buddha-field, after passing through as many buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in forty-two Ganges rivers, there is the Sahā world-system."
There, a Tathāgata named Śākyamuni teaches the Dharma to beings of inferior inclinations in a Buddha-field characterized by the five corruptions.
There, a Bodhisattva named Vimalakīrti, established in the inconceivable liberation, teaches the Dharma to the Bodhisattvas.
By him this emanated Bodhisattva was sent to proclaim my name, to reveal the excellence of this world-system, and to increase the roots of virtue of those Bodhisattvas.
Then those bodhisattvas said:
"Blessed One, how great is that bodhisattva whose emanation has attained such power of supernatural transformations, strength, and fearlessness?
The Blessed One replied:
In the same way, that great-souled bodhisattva dispatches emanations to all buddha-fields,
and those emanations attend to sentient beings by performing the work of a Buddha.
Then the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa, gave that food, which was infused with every fragrance, to that bodhisattva in a vessel scented with every fragrance.
Thereupon, ninety thousand bodhisattvas set out, saying:
"Lord, we shall go to that Sahā world-system to pay homage to the Lord Śākyamuni, and to see Vimalakīrti and those bodhisattvas.
The Lord said:
"Go, sons of good family, at whatever time you deem appropriate.
However, sons of good family, having withdrawn your fragrances, enter that world-system, lest those beings fall into intoxication and negligence."
And withdraw your own form,
lest the beings in the Sahā world-system become dejected,
and lest [it happen] there.
Having conceived the notion of inferiority regarding the realm of sentient beings, you should instead conceive the notion of resistance.
Why is that?
For the fields of the Buddhas are indeed fields of space.
However, for the sake of maturing sentient beings, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, do not reveal their entire Buddha-field.
Then the emanated bodhisattva, taking that food, together with those ninety thousand bodhisattvas,
