through the power of the Buddha and the empowerment of Vimalakīrti, in that very instant, moment, and second, arrived in the world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā.
Having vanished from that world-system, he reappeared in the house of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti.
There, Vimalakīrti miraculously produced ninety thousand lion-thrones, exactly like those first lion-thrones.
Thereupon, those bodhisattvas sat down upon them.
And that emanation presented to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti that vessel filled with food.

By the fragrance of that food, the entire great city of Vaiśālī was perfumed, and even the thousandfold world-system was made fragrant with its sweet scent. Thereupon, the brahmins and householders of Vaiśālī, and Soma-cchattra, the sovereign of the Licchavis, [approached] him...
Having smelled the fragrance, he was struck with wonder and amazement, his body and mind filled with joy, together with eighty-four thousand Licchavis.

And by that very scent of the food, the sons of the gods who dwell on earth, as well as the gods of the desire realm and the form realm, were stirred and approached the house of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said to the Elder Śāriputra and those great śrāvakas:
"Venerable sirs, partake of this ambrosial food of the Tathāgata, which is permeated by great compassion. Do not fix your minds upon a limited practice."
"It is not possible to purify the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Then, some of the disciples thought:
"How will such a vast assembly partake of food from such a meager amount?"
That emanated bodhisattva said this to those śrāvakas:
"Venerable ones, do not attempt to equate the wisdom and merit of the Tathāgata with your own wisdom and merit;
for the four great oceans might reach exhaustion."
Yet there is no exhaustion whatsoever of this food;
even if all sentient beings were to consume it for an eon with mouthfuls as large as Mount Sumeru,
still there would be no depletion of it.
For what reason?
This food remaining in the Tathāgata’s bowl has arisen from inexhaustible morality, concentration, and wisdom; it is not possible to exhaust it.
Then, from that food, the entire assembly was satisfied.
And yet that food was not exhausted.
When those bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, Śakras, Brahmās, world-protectors, and other beings ate that food,
such bliss entered their bodies as is the bliss of the bodhisattvas in the world-system Sarvasukhapratimaṇḍita.
And from all their pores such a fragrance wafts forth,
just like the scent of the trees in that very world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā.
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, knowing full well that those bodhisattvas had come from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Bhagavat Gandhottamakūṭa, addressed them as follows:
"Noble sons, what is the Dharma-teaching of the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa like?
They replied:
"That Tathāgata does not teach the Dharma by means of syllables or verbal expressions."
By that very fragrance those bodhisattvas are disciplined.
Wherever those bodhisattvas sit upon a fragrant tree,
from that very place such a fragrance wafts forth that, as soon as the fragrance is smelled, [there arises] the mine of all the qualities of a bodhisattva.
They attain the concentration by the immediate attainment of which all the qualities of a bodhisattva arise.
Then those bodhisattvas said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"Furthermore, what kind of Dharma teaching does the Blessed One Śākyamuni proclaim here?"
He said: "These beings, O noble sirs, are difficult to tame.
For those beings who are difficult to tame, he reveals only the discourse on the discipline for the wild and the difficult-to-tame.
But what, then, is the discipline for those who are wild and difficult to tame?"
And what is the discourse on the taming of the wild and the difficult-to-subdue?
It is as follows: these hells, this animal realm, and so forth.
This is the world of Yama; these are the unfavorable conditions; this is rebirth with impaired faculties.
This is misconduct of the body;
this is the maturation of misconduct of the body;
this is misconduct of speech.
This is the ripening of verbal misconduct; this is mental misconduct;
this is the ripening of mental misconduct.
This is the taking of life; this is the taking of what is not given;
this is sexual misconduct.
This is false speech;
this is malicious speech; this is harsh speech.
This is frivolous speech,
this is covetousness,
and this is malice.
This is wrong view;
this is their maturation;
this is stinginess.
This is immorality,
this is anger,
this is laziness.
This is distraction; this is faulty wisdom; this is the fruit of faulty wisdom.
This is a transgression of the Prātimokṣa training;
this is the Prātimokṣa;
this is what ought to be done.
This is not to be done; this is the application.
This is the primary factor;
this is the obscuration.
This is unobstructed;
this is an offense; this is not an offense.
This is the emergence from an offense;
this is the path;
this is the wrong path.
This is wholesome; this is unwholesome;
this is blameworthy.
This is blameless;
this is with outflows; this is without outflows.
This is mundane, this is supramundane, this is conditioned.
This is the unconditioned;
this is affliction; this is purification.
"This is saṃsāra; this is nirvāṇa.
By thus instructing them in manifold dharmas, sentient beings whose minds are like wild horses are established [in the path].

Just as a wild horse or an elephant comes to subjection only through the piercing of its vital points, even so here, these unruly and wild beings come to subjection through discourses that revile all forms of suffering.
Those bodhisattvas said:
"How wonderful is the Blessed One Śākyamuni! For having withdrawn his Buddha-majesty, he disciplines unruly beings through poverty and wretchedness.
Even those bodhisattvas who dwell in such a desolate buddha-field possess inconceivable great compassion.
Vimalakīrti said:
In this very way, O noble beings, it is exactly as you say:
even those bodhisattvas who have been reborn here possess firm great compassion.

In this world-system, they will accomplish the welfare of sentient beings to a much greater extent in a single lifetime than could be accomplished for the welfare of sentient beings in that Sarvagandhasugandhā world-system over a thousand eons.
Why is that? Vkn 9.17: Because of this reason.
For here in the Sahā world-system, noble persons possess ten qualities that accumulate merit, which do not exist in other buddha-fields, and which they themselves embrace.
What are the ten? Namely:
gathering [beings] through generosity among the poor, and gathering them through ethical discipline among those of immoral conduct.
The gathering through patience is for those who are hostile;
the gathering through vigor is for those who are indolent;
the gathering through meditative concentration is for those with distracted minds.

The gathering of wisdom among those of poor wisdom; the teaching on transcending the eight unfavorable conditions for those who have attained the favorable condition; and the teaching of the Mahāyāna for those engaged in limited practices.

The gathering of roots of virtue among those who have not yet planted roots of virtue; and the constant and continuous maturation of sentient beings through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*).
They receive these ten dharmas that accumulate virtue, which do not exist in other buddha-fields.
Those bodhisattvas asked:
"Endowed with what qualities does a bodhisattva, having passed away from this Sahā world-system, go to a pure buddha-field, remaining unhurt and uninjured?
Vimalakīrti replied:
Noble son, endowed with eight qualities, a bodhisattva, having passed away from this Sahā world-system, goes to a pure buddha-field unharmed and uninjured.
What are these eight? Namely: "I must bring about the welfare of all sentient beings."
One should not seek any benefit from them;
rather, one must endure all the suffering of all sentient beings, dedicate all roots of virtue to all sentient beings,
and maintain freedom from resentment toward all sentient beings.
Loving all bodhisattvas as one loves the Teacher;
not rejecting teachings heard or not yet heard upon hearing them;
being free from envy regarding the gains of others; and the mental composure that does not become conceited because of one's own gains.
Reflecting upon one’s own lapses, not censuring the transgressions of others, delighting in heedfulness, and undertaking all virtuous qualities—
endowed with these eight dharmas, a bodhisattva, having passed away from this Sahā world-system, goes to a pure buddha-field unhurt and unimpaired.
Now, while that assembly was gathered together, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti and the crown prince Mañjuśrī were present.
As he thus taught the Dharma, the minds of a full thousand living beings were set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment,
and ten thousand bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
The ninth chapter, titled "The Bringing of the Emanated Food."
Now at that time, while the Blessed One was teaching the Dharma in the Āmrapālī grove, that assembly hall became vast and expansive,
and that entire assembly appeared golden in color.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, whose omen is this, that this grove of Āmrapālī has become so vast and established, and that the entire assembly appears golden in color?
The Blessed One replied, “Ānanda, this is the Licchavi Vimalakīrti and the crown prince Mañjuśrī, who, surrounded by a great assembly, are approaching the presence of the Tathāgata.”
Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti said this to the crown prince Mañjuśrī:
“Mañjuśrī, we shall go into the presence of the Blessed One;
these great beings shall see the Tathāgata and pay him homage.”
He said, "Go, noble son; do as you deem it timely.

Then the Licchavi Vimalakīrti performed such a feat of supernatural power (*ṛddhyabhisaṃskāra*) that he placed that entire assembly, together with their lion-thrones, upon his right hand and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and placed that assembly upon the surface of the earth, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated the Blessed One seven times, and stood to one side.
Then those bodhisattvas who had come from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa,
as well as others, descended from their lion-thrones, bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One, and stood to one side.
In this way, Śakra, Brahmā, the World-Protectors, and the sons of the gods bowed their heads at the feet of the Blessed One and stood to one side.
Then the Blessed One, having gladdened those bodhisattvas with a discourse on the Dharma, spoke thus:
"Sit down, sons of good family, each upon your own lion-throne."
Having been permitted by the Blessed One, they sat down.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, have you seen the playful display of these supreme beings, the bodhisattvas?"
He said: "I have seen it, Blessed One.
The Blessed One said:
"What perception then arose in you?"
He said: "O Blessed One, an inconceivable perception arose in me there; I see such an inconceivable activity of theirs that I am unable to conceive of it, weigh it, or calculate it.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, I smell a fragrance such as I have never smelled before."
"Whose is this such fragrance?
He replied: "Ānanda, it is from all the pores of these very bodhisattvas' bodies that this fragrance wafts forth.
Śāriputra also said:
"Venerable Ānanda, such a fragrance also wafts from all our pores.
He asked, "From where does this fragrance originate?
He replied, "The Licchavi Vimalakīrti has brought food from the world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā, the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa."
As long as they had eaten, such a fragrance issued from the bodies of them all.
Then the venerable Ānanda said this to the bodhisattva Vimalakīrti: "Noble son, for how long will this fragrance persist?"
He said: "As long as this food has not been digested.
Ānanda asked: "But how long will it take for this food to be digested?
He replied: "It will be digested in seven times seven days."
Furthermore, for seven days thereafter, his vital energy will radiate,

and he shall suffer no ill effects from indigestion. Reverend Ānanda, as for those monks who have not yet entered the fixed course of certainty and have eaten this food, it will be digested once they have entered that fixed course.
Furthermore, for those who have entered the fixed course of certainty (*niyāma*) and have eaten it, it will not digest until their minds are fully liberated.

For those beings who have not yet generated the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and have consumed it, it will digest once they have generated the thought of awakening. For those who have generated the thought of awakening and have eaten it, it will not digest until they have attained patient acceptance (*kṣānti*).
Furthermore, for those who have attained *kṣānti* and have eaten [this food], it will be digested when they are bound to only one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).

Reverend Ānanda, it is just as if there were a medicine called "Delicious" (*svādu*): once it has entered the stomach, it does not digest until all the poison that pervades the body has been eliminated.
Thereafter, that medicine is digested.
In the same way, venerable Ānanda, that food remains undigested until the poison of all afflictions has been rendered non-poisonous;
thereafter, that food is digested.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, this food performs the work of a Buddha.
He replied: "It is so, Ānanda, it is so, just as you say."
Ānanda, there are buddha-fields in which bodhisattvas perform the work of a Buddha;
there are buddha-fields in which the tree of enlightenment performs the work of a Buddha;
and there are buddha-fields in which the vision of the Tathāgata’s physical marks and form performs the work of a Buddha.
In this way, the sky and the atmosphere perform the work of a Buddha;
such is the discipline of those beings.

Likewise, the explanations through the analysis of syllables and the presentation of metaphors—such as dreams, reflections, the moon in water, echoes, illusions, and mirages—perform the work of a Buddha for sentient beings.

There are, Ānanda, buddha-fields where the communication of syllables performs the work of a Buddha. There are, Ānanda, such utterly pure buddha-fields where non-utterance, non-proclamation, non-indication, and ineffability perform the work of a Buddha for those beings.
Ānanda, there is no posture whatsoever and no enjoyment whatsoever that does not perform the work of a Buddha for the sake of disciplining beings by the Blessed Buddhas.
Ānanda, these four Māras and the eighty-four thousand gateways of affliction by which sentient beings are defiled—
all these are used by the Buddha Bhagavāns to perform the work of a Buddha.
Ānanda, this is the gateway to the Dharma called "Entry into All Buddha-Dharmas," in whichever gateway to the Dharma...
Having entered, the Bodhisattva is neither discouraged nor humbled by those Buddha-fields endowed with all magnificent arrays of qualities;
nor is he attracted to or elated by those Buddha-fields endowed with all magnificent arrays of qualities.
Furthermore, in the presence of the Tathāgatas, he generates an exceeding degree of reverence.
This is a marvel of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, who are resolved upon the equality of all phenomena, yet display a diversity of Buddha-fields for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
Ānanda, it is just as there is a diversity of various qualities among Buddha-fields, but no diversity in the space that covers the path of the birds— that is, the space of the Buddha-field itself.
In the same way, Ānanda, there is a diversity among the Tathāgatas in their physical bodies,
but there is no diversity among the Tathāgatas in their unimpeded gnosis.
For, Ānanda, all Buddhas are equal in form, complexion, splendor, physique, marks, and the greatness of their lineage.

By means of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, the powers, the grounds of self-confidence, the unique qualities of a Buddha, great loving-kindness, great compassion, the desire for the welfare of others, proper deportment, conduct, the path, the lifespan, the teaching of the Dharma, the ripening of sentient beings, the liberation of sentient beings, the purification of the buddha-field, and the complete fulfillment of all the qualities of a Buddha.
Therefore, he is called the *samyaksaṃbuddha*, the *tathāgata*, and the *buddha*.
Ānanda, even if you were to remain for an entire *kalpa*, it would not be easy for you to fully master the detailed explanation and analysis of the meaning of these three terms.

Furthermore, Ānanda, suppose all the beings included within the triple-thousandfold world system were like you—foremost among those who have heard much and have attained the power of memory and retention.

Even if all those beings were equal to Ānanda, having attained the retention of what is heard and remembered, they would not be able—even in an eon—to explain the determination of the meaning of these three terms:
namely, "Perfectly Enlightened One," "Tathāgata," and "Buddha.
For thus, Ānanda, the awakening of a Buddha is immeasurable.
Such is the inconceivable wisdom and eloquence of the Tathāgatas.
Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"From this day forward, Blessed One, I shall no longer claim for myself the preeminence among those who have heard much."
The Blessed One said: "Do not, Ānanda, give rise to a discouraged mind.
For what reason? Because..."
"Ānanda, it was with reference to the śrāvakas that I designated you as the foremost among those who have heard much, not with reference to the bodhisattvas.
Let the bodhisattvas be, Ānanda."
These cannot be fathomed by a wise person.
For, Ānanda, while it is possible to measure the depth of all the oceans,
it is not at all possible to measure the depth of the wisdom, knowledge, mindfulness, dhāraṇīs, and eloquence of the bodhisattvas.
"Ānanda, you should remain indifferent toward the conduct of a bodhisattva.
Why is that?
Ānanda, these arrays which have been displayed by the Licchavi Vimalakīrti in a single morning meal—"

They could not be displayed by all the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who have attained supernatural powers, even through all their miraculous transformations and wonders throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas.
Then, those bodhisattvas who had come from the world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā— the buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Gandhottamakūṭa—
all joined their palms in reverence and paid homage to the Tathāgata.
And they spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, we renounce those mental orientations by which we conceived a notion of inferiority toward this buddha-field.
For what reason? Because—"
"Indeed, Blessed One, the Buddha-realm of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, is inconceivable.
Through skill in means for the sake of maturing sentient beings, they manifest arrays of fields in whatever way they desire.
Blessed One, grant us a gift of Dharma so that, having gone to that world-system Sarvagandhasugandhā, we may remember the Blessed One."
The Blessed One said:
"Noble sons, there is a liberation of bodhisattvas called 'the exhaustible and the inexhaustible. In that regard, you must train yourselves."
Furthermore, what is that?
The conditioned is called "exhaustible," and the unconditioned is "inexhaustible."
Therefore, a bodhisattva should neither exhaust the conditioned nor abide in the unconditioned.
In this regard, the inexhaustibility of the conditioned is as follows:
That is to say: the non-falling away from great loving-kindness, the non-abandonment of great compassion,
and the non-forgetfulness of the mind of omniscience set forth through resolute intention.
tirelessness in maturing sentient beings, not abandoning the means of attraction, and the relinquishing of body and life for the sake of upholding the true Dharma.
Insatiable longing for roots of virtue, establishment in skill in dedication,
and lack of indolence in the search for the Dharma.
Having no "teacher's fist" (secretiveness) regarding the teaching of the Dharma;
zeal for the sight of the Tathāgata and for the objects of worship; and being without fear regarding intentional rebirths.
Neither elation in prosperity nor depression in adversity;
no contempt for those who are untrained,
and affection toward those who are trained as if toward the Teacher himself.
The application of proper reflection toward those overwhelmed by afflictions,
a lack of absorption in the pleasures of solitude,
and no attachment to one's own happiness.
Being absorbed in the happiness of others;
perceiving even the meditative absorptions, concentrations, and attainments as the Avīci hell; and perceiving cyclic existence as a pleasure grove or celestial palace.
The perception of those who beg as spiritual friends;
the perception of the perfection of omniscience in the relinquishment of all possessions;
and the perception of protection toward those of immoral conduct.
The perception of the perfections as one's parents;
the perception of the factors conducive to awakening as one's own retinue;
and the inexhaustible accumulation of all roots of merit.
The accomplishment of one’s own buddha-field through the qualities of all buddha-fields;
the performance of unobstructed sacrifices for the sake of perfecting the primary and secondary marks;
and the adornment of body, speech, and mind through the non-committal of any evil.

Wandering through incalculable eons with the complete purity of body, speech, and mind; not becoming despondent upon hearing of the immeasurable qualities of the Buddhas due to the courage of one's mind;
and grasping the weapon of wisdom in order to subdue the enemy of the afflictions.
The thorough knowledge of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases for the sake of bearing the burden of all sentient beings;
ardent vigor for the purpose of subduing the armies of Māra; and freedom from pride for the seeking of the Dharma.

Seeking knowledge while maintaining receptivity toward the Dharma is contentment with few desires; being beloved by all the world while remaining unsullied by any worldly phenomena is detachment from all worldly things; and conforming to the ways of the world while remaining undisturbed in all modes of conduct is the preservation of proper deportment.

The production of supernormal knowledges for the purpose of demonstrating all activities; the possession of the knowledge of retention, mindfulness, and wisdom for the purpose of retaining all that has been heard;
and the knowledge of the superior and inferior faculties of beings for the purpose of cutting through the doubts of all sentient beings.
The state of being an unattached basis for the teaching of the Dharma; the state of unattached eloquence through the attainment of the acquisition of inspired speech;
and the experience of the prosperity of gods and humans through the purification of the ten wholesome paths of action.

Establishment in the path of Brahmā is for the sake of generating the four immeasurables; the attainment of the voice of a Buddha is through requesting [others] to teach the Dharma, rejoicing in it, and offering praise;
and the attainment of the deportment of a Buddha is through the excellence of restraint in body, speech, and mind, and by not being absorbed in any phenomena.
By attracting the community of bodhisattvas, one encourages others toward the Mahāyāna;
and by ensuring that all virtues are not lost, one practices heedfulness.
For in this way, noble sons, a bodhisattva who is devoted to these dharmas does not exhaust the conditioned.
Furthermore, how does one not abide in the unconditioned?
It is when one practices the mastery of emptiness,
yet does not personally realize emptiness.
He masters the signless,
yet he does not personally realize the signless;
he masters the wishless, yet...
He does not realize the wishless,
yet he masters the absence of volitional formation;
he does not, however, realize the absence of volitional formation.
He contemplates that "it is impermanent," yet he is not satiated with his roots of virtue;
he contemplates that "it is suffering," yet...
He is reborn intentionally,
and he contemplates "non-self," yet he does not abandon the nature of self.
He contemplates that it is "peaceful," yet he does not bring about ultimate peace;
he contemplates that it is "secluded."
One exerts oneself with both body and mind;
one contemplates that there is no abiding,
yet one does not abandon the abode of pure dharmas.
He contemplates non-appropriation,
yet he bears the burden taken up for the sake of sentient beings;
he contemplates the untainted, yet...
He enters into the process of saṃsāra, yet he contemplates its lack of movement; nevertheless,
he moves about for the sake of maturing sentient beings.
He contemplates selflessness, yet does not abandon great compassion for sentient beings; he contemplates non-arising, yet...
He does not fall into the fixed destiny of the śrāvaka;
he contemplates that [the world] is empty, vain, essence-less, ownerless, and without abode,
yet his merit is not empty.

He possesses non-empty knowledge, his intentions are fulfilled, he is consecrated by self-existent wisdom (*svayambhūjñāna*), he is devoted to self-existent wisdom, he has realized the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and he is established in the lineage of the Buddhas.
For it is thus, noble sons, that a bodhisattva who is thus resolved upon the Dharma does not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because of his devotion to the accumulation of merit (*puṇyasaṃbhāra*), he does not abide in the unconditioned.
Because he is devoted to the accumulation of wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned;
because he is endowed with great loving-kindness, he does not rest in the unconditioned; and because he is endowed with great compassion, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because of maturing sentient beings, one does not abide in the unconditioned;
because of longing for the Buddha-qualities, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because of fulfilling the marks of a Buddha, one does not abide in the unconditioned.
For the sake of fulfilling the knowledge of omniscience, he does not exhaust the conditioned;
because of his skill in means, he does not rest in the unconditioned;
and because of his thorough investigation through wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
For the sake of purifying the buddha-field, he does not rest in the unconditioned;
because of the Buddha’s empowerment, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because he experiences the welfare of sentient beings, he does not rest in the unconditioned.
Because he clearly perceives the meaning of the Dharma, he does not exhaust the conditioned;
because he possesses the equipment of the roots of virtue, he does not abide in the unconditioned;
and because he is permeated by the impressions of the roots of virtue, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
For the sake of fulfilling his vows, he does not rest in the unconditioned;
because of his wishlessness, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because of the purity of his intention, he does not rest in the unconditioned.
Because his resolute intention is completely pure, he does not exhaust the conditioned;
because he sports with the five supernormal knowledges, he does not abide in the unconditioned;
and because he possesses the six supernormal knowledges of a Buddha’s wisdom, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
For the sake of fulfilling the equipment of the perfections (*pāramitā-saṃbhāra*), he does not rest in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
because the time is not yet complete, he does not exhaust the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Because he gathers the wealth of the Dharma, he does not rest in the unconditioned.
Because he does not seek partial dharmas, he does not exhaust the conditioned;
because he gathers all medicinal herbs, he does not rest in the unconditioned;
and because he applies the medicine according to what is appropriate, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because of his firm vow, he does not rest in the unconditioned;
because he fulfills his vow, he does not exhaust the conditioned.
Because he procures the medicine of the Dharma, he does not rest in the unconditioned.
Just as one does not exhaust the conditioned because of the application of even a small amount of the medicine of the Dharma;
nor does one abide in the unconditioned because of the thorough knowledge of the diseases of the afflictions of all sentient beings;
[and] because of the pacification of all diseases, one does not exhaust the conditioned.
In this way, noble sons, a bodhisattva does not exhaust the conditioned,
nor does he abide in the unconditioned. This is called the liberation of bodhisattvas known as "the indestructible destruction."
"In this regard, O noble sons, you must apply yourselves with diligence.

Then, having heard this instruction, those bodhisattvas were satisfied, elated, joyful, and filled with gladness and happiness; they arose to perform acts of worship for the Blessed One and for those bodhisattvas.

In order to perform an act of worship for this Dharma discourse, they covered this entire great trichiliocosm to the depth of the knees with arrays of all kinds of powdered incenses, perfumes, and flowers, as well as blossoms; having strewn them over the circle of the Blessed One’s assembly,
bowed their heads at the Blessed One’s feet, and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, they uttered this inspired utterance here in this Buddha-field:
In that very instant, moment, and second, they vanished from there and reappeared in that world-system called Sarvagandhasugandhā.
The tenth chapter, titled "The Exhaustible and the Inexhaustible," from the *Dharmaprābhṛta*.
Then the Blessed One said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"Noble son, when you desire to see the Tathāgata, how do you perceive the Tathāgata?"
When this had been said, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti addressed the Blessed One as follows:
"Blessed One, whenever I desire to see the Tathāgata, I then see the Tathāgata by way of non-seeing."
I see it as unarisen from the past, untransferred to the future, and non-abiding in the present time.
Why is that? Because its nature is the suchness of form, which is formless.
The nature of the suchness of feeling is non-feeling; the nature of the suchness of perception is non-perception;
the nature of the suchness of mental formations is non-formation.
It has the nature of the suchness of consciousness, yet is non-consciousness;
it does not belong to the four elements and is equal to the element of space;

it is unarisen in the six sense bases and transcends the path of the eye, transcends the path of the ear, transcends the path of the nose, transcends the path of the tongue, and transcends the path of the body.
Unmixed with the three realms,
free from the three stains,
and followed by the three liberations.
It has attained the three knowledges; it is unattained yet fully attained;
it has reached the limit of non-attachment regarding all phenomena; it is the limit of reality that is itself without a limit.
It is established in suchness, mutually dissociated from one another;
it is not produced by causes, nor dependent on conditions;
it is neither of different characteristics nor of identical characteristics.
It has neither a single characteristic nor manifold characteristics;
it is not perceived, not fully perceived, and not distinguished; it is neither on this side, nor on the far side, nor in between.
Neither here nor there, neither from this nor from another;
it is not to be known by cognition, nor is it established in consciousness.
It is without darkness and without light; it is nameless and signless; it is neither weak nor strong.
It does not abide in a place, nor does it abide in a region;
it is neither auspicious nor inauspicious,
neither conditioned nor unconditioned.
Nor can he be described by any particular attribute,
neither in terms of generosity nor in terms of stinginess,
neither in terms of ethical discipline nor in terms of immorality.
Neither from patience nor from malice,
neither from vigor nor from indolence,
neither from meditative concentration nor from distraction.
Neither through wisdom nor through lack of wisdom; neither expressible nor inexpressible;
neither from the perspective of truth nor from the perspective of falsehood.
It is neither leading to deliverance nor not leading to deliverance;
it is neither approachable nor unapproachable,
for all vocal expression and discourse have been utterly severed.
He is neither a field nor a non-field;
he is neither worthy of offerings nor a purifier of offerings;
he is ungraspable.
Untouched, homeless, unconditioned.
Beyond number,
equal through equanimity, and identical through the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
Of incomparable vigor,
transcending all comparison,
neither having stepped forward nor not having stepped forward.
It has not been transcended,
nor has it been seen, heard, or fully known;
it is free from all knots.
He has attained equality with the wisdom of the omniscient one;
he is equal toward all sentient beings;
and he has attained the state in which all phenomena are without distinction.
Blameless in every respect, free from possessions, and free from passion.
Partless,
free from conceptual construction, and unconditioned.
Unborn, unarisen, and non-existent.
Unarisen, he will not come into being;
he is fearless.
Free from afflictions, free from sorrow, and free from joy.
Free from waves,
it is inexpressible by any conventional designations;
such, O Blessed One, is the body of the Tathāgata.
It should be viewed in that very way;
those who see it thus, they see correctly.
But those who see otherwise, they see falsely.
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, from which buddha-field did the noble son Vimalakīrti pass away before coming to this buddha-field?
The Blessed One said:
“Śāriputra, ask this very good man himself: ‘From where did you pass away to be reborn here?’”
Then the venerable Śāriputra said this to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
"Noble son, from where did you pass away to be reborn here? Vimalakīrti replied:
"Regarding the Dharma that has been realized by the Elder,
is there any falling away from or arising of that Dharma?
He replied, "There is no falling away from or arising of that Dharma whatsoever."

He said: "Venerable Śāriputra, since all phenomena are thus without passing away and without arising, how can it occur to you to ask: 'From where have you passed away to be reborn here? Venerable Śāriputra, if you were to ask a magically created woman or man, 'From where have you passed away to be reborn here,' what would he say?"
He said: "Noble son, for a magical creation there is neither death nor rebirth;
what, then, will it predict?
He replied: "But, Reverend Śāriputra, has the Tathāgata not taught that all phenomena have the nature of a magical creation?"
He said: "It is so, noble son.
He said: "Venerable Śāriputra, since all phenomena have the nature of being magically created, from where have you passed away to be reborn here?
Venerable Śāriputra, 'passing away' is a term for the characteristic of the moment of volitional formation."
"Rebirth" refers to this continuity of conditioned formations (*abhisaṃskāra*).
In that regard, the bodhisattva passes away,
yet he does not exhaust the formation of roots of virtue.
He is reborn,
yet he does not bind himself to unwholesome states.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, this son of good family has come from the presence of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya in the world-system Abhirati.
He said, "It is marvelous, Blessed One, that this virtuous man, having come from such a completely pure Buddha-field, takes delight here in a Buddha-field so corrupted by many defects.
Vimalakīrti said:
"What do you think, Venerable Śāriputra? Do the rays of the sun ever take pleasure in the company of darkness? He replied, "Certainly not, noble son; there is no union between the two."
For as soon as the solar disc has risen, all darkness departs.
He asked: "For what reason, then, does the sun rise over Jambūdvīpa?
He replied: "Precisely for the purpose of providing illumination and for the destruction of darkness."
He said: "In just this way, Śāriputra, Bodhisattvas intentionally take birth in impure Buddha-fields for the sake of purifying sentient beings.
Yet they do not dwell together with the afflictions (kleśas), and they dispel the darkness of the afflictions for all sentient beings."
Then that entire assembly became filled with longing, thinking:
"May we behold that world-system Abhirati, that Tathāgata Akṣobhya, those bodhisattvas, and those great śrāvakas!
Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in the minds of that entire assembly, addressed the Licchavi Vimalakīrti as follows:
"O son of good family, show this assembly that world-system Abhirati and that Tathāgata Akṣobhya;
this assembly wishes to see them. Then, this thought occurred to the Licchavi Vimalakīrti:
What if I were not to rise from this seat,
[but remain] in that world-system Abhirati, which contains many hundreds of thousands of bodhisattvas, is inhabited by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and asuras,
and includes its encircling walls and moats, its rivers, ponds, springs, lakes, and oceans, and its Mount Sumerus, peaks, and mountains?
Together with the light of the moon and sun; together with the abodes of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas; together with the assembly surrounding the abode of Brahmā;
together with villages, cities, market towns, provinces, kingdoms, and human beings; together with women’s quarters; together with the assembly of bodhisattvas and śrāvakas;
[he saw] the Bodhi tree of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
And he saw the Tathāgata Akṣobhya seated in a great assembly like the ocean, teaching the Dharma;
he also saw those lotuses which perform the work of a Buddha for sentient beings in the ten directions,
as well as those three staircases made of jewels that extend from Jambūdvīpa up to the abode of the Thirty-three Gods.

By means of these ascending stairways, the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three descend to Jambudvīpa to behold, pay homage to, attend upon, and listen to the Dharma from the Tathāgata Akṣobhya; and the humans of Jambudvīpa ascend to the abode of the Thirty-Three to behold the gods of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three.

Having thus cut out that world-system Abhirati, which is endowed with immeasurable qualities— from its mass of water up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven— like a potter’s wheel, and having taken it with my right hand like a garland of flowers, I would bring it into this world-system; and having brought it in, I would show it to this entire assembly.

Then, at that time, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti entered such a meditative concentration and performed such a miraculous feat that, having cut out the world-system Abhirati, he took it with his right hand and brought it into this Sahā world-system.

Thereupon, those disciples and bodhisattvas who had attained the supernormal power of the divine eye, as well as gods and humans, raised a great cry: "We are undone, O Blessed One! We are undone, O Sugata!"
"Protect us, O Tathāgata! To them, for the sake of disciplining them, the Blessed One said this:
"I have no such prowess here as that which is being displayed by the bodhisattva Vimalakīrti."
Furthermore, as for the other gods and humans there,
they did not know and did not see from where they were being brought;
for when the world-system Abhirati was made to enter this Sahā world-system, there was neither deficiency nor fullness.
There was neither compression nor congestion in this world-system, nor did the world-system Abhirati suffer any depletion;
it appeared exactly as it had been before.
Then the Blessed One Śākyamuni addressed that entire assembly:
"Behold, sirs, the world-system Abhirati, the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, and these arrays of fields, these arrays of disciples, and these arrays of bodhisattvas!
They replied: "We see them, Blessed One."
He said: "Friends, a bodhisattva who wishes to take hold of such a buddha-field should train in the bodhisattva-conduct of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.

Furthermore, through this miraculous display of supernatural power that revealed the world-system Abhirati and the manifestation of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya, fourteen nayutas of the human and divine populations in this Sahā world-system [were established] in the unsurpassed..."
They have conceived the aspiration for perfect enlightenment,
and all of them have formed the vow to be reborn in the world-system Abhirati;
the Blessed One has prophesied that they shall all be reborn in the world-system Abhirati.

Thus, the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, having performed all that was necessary for the maturation of sentient beings here in this Sahā world-system, restored that Abhirati world-system to its original place. Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra:
"Śāriputra, have you seen that world-system Abhirati and that Tathāgata Akṣobhya? He replied, "I have seen them, Blessed One.
May all sentient beings possess such arrays of qualities in their Buddha-fields."
"May all sentient beings be endowed with such supernatural power as that of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti, the son of good family!
And may we also find our gains well-acquired,
we who have obtained the sight of such holy men."
Those beings, too, will have gained a great gain,
who at this time shall hear this Dharma-discourse, whether while the Tathāgata is staying or after he has passed into parinirvāṇa;
what need is there to mention others?
Those who, having heard it, will have faith in it, will trust in it, will take it up, will retain it, will recite it,

will master it, will resolve upon it, will propagate it, and will reveal it in detail to others, and who will become devoted to the practice of its cultivation— [for them, this merit shall be even greater].
Those into whose hands this Dharma discourse shall fall will have attained the treasure-store of the Dharma;
they will be companions of the Tathāgata.
Those who shall recite this Dharma discourse will become guardians of the Dharma;
they will provide service and attendance to those who are devoted to this Dharma.
The Tathāgata will be present in the homes of those who, having well-written this Dharma-discourse, shall uphold it and honor it;
they shall be embraced by all merit.
Those who rejoice in this Dharma discourse will perform a great Dharma-sacrifice; those who,
from this Dharma discourse, shall teach even a single four-line verse or a single precept to others in detail.
Blessed One, that itself is the prediction for those who shall possess patience, delight, intelligence, discernment, vision, resolve, and liberation regarding this Dharma-discourse.
The eleventh chapter: Bringing the Abhirati World System and Beholding the Tathāgata Akṣobhya.
Then Śakra, the lord of the gods, said this to the Blessed One:
“Blessed One, I have heard hundreds of thousands of Dharma discourses from the Tathāgata and from Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta;
yet never before have I heard such an entrance into the method of the Dharma and the miraculous transformations of the inconceivable liberation as is taught here in this Dharma discourse.”
Without doubt, those beings who shall take up, uphold, recite, and master this Dharma discourse will become such vessels for the Dharma;
what need is there to mention others?
For those who will be devoted to the practice of meditation,
all miserable realms are closed to them, and all paths to happy rebirths are opened for them.
They have been seen by all the Buddhas;
they have defeated all those who propound opposing doctrines;
they have conquered all Māras.
The paths to awakening have been purified by them;
they are established upon the seat of awakening (bodhimaṇḍa) and shall come to abide in the state of the Tathāgata.
“Blessed One, I too, together with my entire retinue, shall provide service and attendance for those noble sons who uphold this Dharma discourse.
And in whatever villages, towns, market towns, districts, kingdoms, or royal capitals this Dharma discourse circulates, is taught, and is proclaimed,”
There I shall approach, together with my retinue, to listen to the Dharma;
I shall inspire faith in those sons of good family who have no faith,
and I shall provide righteous protection, defense, and guardianship for those who already have faith.
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to Śakra, the lord of the gods: "Excellent, excellent, Lord of the Gods!
The Tathāgata rejoices in what you have well spoken."
O Devendra, that awakening of the past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, which has been taught here in this Dharma-discourse—

from that [teaching], O Devendra, those past, future, and present Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, will have been honored by that son of good family or daughter of good family who shall take up this Dharma-discourse, or even cause it to be written in a book, or read it, write it out, or master it.

Furthermore, O Lord of Devas, if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to honor, revere, and respect this trichiliocosm— filled with Tathāgatas as densely as a grove of sugarcane, or a grove of reeds, or a grove of bamboo, or a grove of sesame, or a grove of rice— for an eon or for the remainder of an eon;
One should worship those Tathāgatas with all forms of worship and all articles of comfort;

and for the sake of worshipping each single one of those Tathāgatas who have entered parinirvāṇa, one should establish for their solid, unfragmented body a stūpa made of every kind of jewel, equal in size to a world-system of four great continents.
Extending as high as the Brahma-world, adorned with uplifted poles, parasols, and banners— one should cause a stūpa to be built for each of all the Tathāgatas in this manner;

and there, for an eon or the remainder of an eon, one should perform worship with all kinds of flowers, all kinds of perfumes, all kinds of flags and banners, and the sounding of all musical instruments and cymbals.
"What do you think, Indra, Lord of the Gods? Would that son of good family or daughter of good family produce much merit on that account?
He replied: "Much, Blessed One; much, Sugata.
It would not be possible to reach the limit of that mass of merit even in hundreds of thousands of millions of eons."
The Blessed One said:
"I announce to you, O Lord of Gods; I declare to you."

Therefore, that son of good family or daughter of good family would generate much more merit who would take up, maintain, recite, and master this Dharma discourse, the Instruction on the Inconceivable Liberation.
Why is that?
For, O Lord of Gods, the awakening of the Blessed Buddhas is born of the Dharma;
it can be honored only by means of the Dharma, not by material things.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, you should understand it in this way through this very method.
Long ago, O Lord of Gods, in the past, in an aeon that was incalculable, more than incalculable,

vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable— during that time and at that moment— there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the world, an unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, named Bhaiṣajyarāja.
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One, [lived] in the world-system Mahāvyūha during the eon Viśodhana.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, the lifespan of that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyarāja was twenty intermediate eons (antarakalpa).
His community of disciples consisted of thirty-six koṭī-niyutas.
There was an assembly of twelve koṭis of bodhisattvas.
And at that time, O Devendra, during that very period, there was a king named Ratnacchattra, a universal monarch endowed with the seven jewels and lord of the four continents;
he had a full thousand sons who were heroic, possessed of excellent forms, and crushers of enemy armies.
Furthermore, at that time, King Ratnacchattra honored the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, along with his retinue, for five intermediate kalpas with every provision for comfort.
Thus, O Lord of the Gods, at the conclusion of those five intermediate kalpas, King Ratnacchattra addressed his thousand sons:
"Know this, sirs!"
"I have performed worship to the Tathāgata;
now you, too, perform worship to the Tathāgata.
Thus, O Indra, those princes, having replied "Very well" to their father, King Ratnacchattra, [proceeded to do so].
All together, in full assembly, for another five intermediate eons, they honored that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, with all the requisites of happiness.
Then there was one prince named Somacchatra.
As he was alone and in seclusion, this thought occurred to him:
"Is there perhaps another noble offering that is more distinguished than this offering?
Then, through the empowerment of the Buddha, a deity spoke to him from the sky:
"O noble son, the Dharma-worship excels all other forms of worship.
He asked: "What, then, is that Dharma-worship?
The deity said: "Noble son, go to this very Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja and ask him: 'What is that Dharma-worship?'"
"The Blessed One will explain it to you.
Then, O Indra, Lord of the Gods, the prince Somacchattra approached the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Bhaiṣajyarāja.
Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One and stood to one side.
Standing to one side, Prince Somacchatra addressed the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, saying:
"Blessed One, it is said, 'Dharma-worship, Dharma-worship. What is this Dharma-worship?"
The Blessed One said: "Noble son, the worship of the Dharma consists in [the practice directed toward] those discourses spoken by the Tathāgata which are profound, which illuminate the profound,
which are contrary to all the world, and which are difficult to fathom, difficult to see, difficult to realize, subtle, and precise."
[They are] those that are beyond apprehension, contained within the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, sealed with the seal of the king of dhāraṇīs and sūtras, indicating the wheel of non-retrogression,

born from the six perfections, comprised of what is to be grasped, following the factors conducive to awakening, bringing forth the limbs of awakening, providing entry into great compassion for sentient beings, teaching great loving-kindness, free from the views and states of Māra, and expounded as dependent origination.
They are devoid of self, devoid of sentient beings, devoid of life-force, and devoid of persons; they are characterized by emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of volitional effort;
they bring about the seat of awakening and set in motion the wheel of Dharma; they are praised and extolled by gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas;

they ensure that the lineage of the true Dharma is not interrupted and preserve the treasury of the Dharma; they have entered into the supreme worship of the Dharma and are embraced by all noble beings.

They are the instructors of the conduct of all bodhisattvas; they lead others into the collection of the Dharma of ultimate reality; they arise from the summaries of the Dharma—impermanence, suffering, selflessness, and peace; they strike down the pride of those with immoral conduct; they terrify all opponents, those of evil views, and those who are attached to the notion of objective existence; they are praised by all Buddhas; they are the adversaries of saṃsāra; and they reveal the bliss of nirvāṇa.
The teaching, the proclamation, the upholding, the contemplation, and the gathering of the true Dharma of such sūtras as these—
this is called the "Dharma-worship. Furthermore, noble son, the Dharma-worship is that which consists in the profound reflection upon the dharmas within the dharmas.
The practice of the Dharma,
conformity with dependent origination,
and the departure from all extreme views.
The patient acceptance of the unborn and unarisen; the entry into selflessness and the absence of sentient beings;
and non-contradiction regarding causes and conditions.
absence of conflict, absence of dispute,
and the state of being free from the sense of "mine."
The disappearance of the sense of "mine," relying on the meaning rather than the letter,
and relying on direct knowledge rather than discursive consciousness.
Relying on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) rather than adhering to the conventional reality of those requiring interpretation (*neyārtha*);
relying on the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) rather than perceiving a person (*pudgala*) or being attached to objects of apprehension (*grāhya*),
thus following phenomena as they truly are.
It is the entrance into the non-abode,
the eradication of the storehouse-consciousness,
the subsiding of ignorance, and so on, up to the subsiding of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, depression, and despair.

And thus he contemplates the twelvefold dependent origination; he brings it forth through inexhaustible accomplishment, and, out of regard for sentient beings, he remains independent of [wrong] views.

"Noble son, this too is called the unsurpassed worship of the Dharma. Thus, O Lord of the Gods, having heard this worship of the Dharma from the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, Prince Somacchatra attained the patient acceptance that accords with the Dharma (*anulomikī dharma-kṣānti*).
Covering the Blessed One with the garments and ornaments he was wearing,
he spoke these words:
"Blessed One, I am able to uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, to perform worship of the True Dharma, and to protect the True Dharma."
“May the Blessed One grant me such an empowerment that, having struck down Māra and my adversaries, I may uphold the True Dharma of the Blessed One.
Knowing his high resolve, that Tathāgata prophesied that he would protect and guard the city of the True Dharma in the final age.

Furthermore, Devānām Indra, while that Tathāgata was still living, Prince Somacchattra, having out of faith gone forth from the home to the homeless life, dwelt with energy aroused toward wholesome qualities.
By means of that aroused energy and being established in wholesome qualities, he soon produced the five superknowledges (*pañcābhijñā*).
Having attained mastery over the dhāraṇīs, he possessed an uninterrupted eloquence.

After that Blessed One had passed into parinirvāṇa, by the power of his superknowledges and dhāraṇīs, he continued to turn the wheel of Dharma set in motion by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja, for a full ten intermediate kalpas.

Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, by that monk Somacchattra, who was devoted to upholding the True Dharma, one billion beings were rendered irreversible from unexcelled [enlightenment], fourteen million living beings were established in the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas,
and immeasurable beings were caused to attain rebirth in the heavens.
Furthermore, O Lord of Gods, you might think that at that time and on that occasion the universal monarch named Ratnacchattra was someone else;
however, O Lord of Gods, you should not view it in this way.
And for what reason?
At that time, on that occasion, the Tathāgata Ratnārcis was the universal monarch named King Ratnacchatra.
Furthermore, those who were the thousand sons of King Ratnacchatra were these very Bodhisattvas of the Auspicious Aeon (Bhadrakalpa).

In this Fortunate Aeon (*bhadrakalpa*), a full thousand Buddhas will arise; of these, four have already arisen, while the remainder are yet to arise, beginning with Krakucchanda and ending with Rocana.
The Tathāgata named Rocana will be the last.

Furthermore, O Śakra, Lord of the Devas, it might occur to you that the prince named Somacchattra at that time and on that occasion was someone other than [myself] who upheld the true Dharma of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyarāja.
But indeed, you should not view it in that way.
For what reason?
At that time, on that occasion, I was the prince named Somacchatra.
Therefore, O Lord of Gods, by this very method you should understand it thus.
"Of all the offerings made to the Tathāgatas, the offering of the Dharma is declared to be the foremost;
it is called the eldest, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the most refined, the highest, and the unsurpassed."
Therefore, O Indra, Lord of the Gods, honor me here with the worship of the Dharma, not with the worship of material things;
honor me with the veneration of the Dharma.
"Not for the sake of material gain or honor.
Then the Blessed One addressed the Bodhisattva Maitreya:
"Maitreya, I entrust to you this unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, which I have accomplished over the course of incalculable millions of eons."

So that such Dharma-discourses as these, through your empowerment and protection, may be widely disseminated in Jambudvīpa during the final period, the final time after the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa,
and not allowed to disappear.
For what reason?

"Maitreya, in a future time there will be sons of good family and daughters of good family, as well as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas, who have planted roots of merit and have set out for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
lest they should fall away due to not hearing this Dharma-discourse,
they shall, upon hearing such sūtras as these, attain exceedingly great love and serene faith."
And they will receive them upon their heads.
Maitreya, for the sake of protecting such sons of good family and daughters of good family as those, you should at that time cause these sūtras of this kind to be widely disseminated.
Maitreya, there are these two seals of the bodhisattvas.
Which two?
The seal of clarity regarding diverse words and phrases, and the seal of entering into the realization of reality as it is, without being terrified by the profound method of the Dharma.
Maitreya, these are the two seals of the bodhisattvas.
In this regard, Maitreya, those bodhisattvas who place their trust in and value diverse words and phrases should be known as beginner bodhisattvas.

However, Maitreya, those who shall set forth, hear, have faith in, and experience this profound sūtra— which is unstained by form and distinguished by its delivery of paired and inverted phrases— [they are not beginners].
These bodhisattvas should be known as those who have long practiced the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
In this regard, Maitreya, beginner bodhisattvas ruin themselves for two reasons and do not attain conviction in the profound teachings.
By which two?
Having heard profound sūtras never heard before, they become terrified and fall into doubt.
They do not rejoice; furthermore, they reject it, saying:
"These things which we have never heard before—whence have they come now?"
And those sons of good family who are upholders of the profound sūtras of the Dharma, who are vessels for the profound Dharma, and who are teachers of the profound Dharma—
they do not serve them, do not associate with them, do not attend upon them,
and they show them no respect.
And from time to time, they even utter disparagement toward them.
Maitreya, by these two causes, beginner bodhisattvas ruin themselves and do not attain deep conviction regarding profound dharmas.
“Maitreya, for two reasons a bodhisattva who is devoted to the profound exhausts himself and does not attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena. What are these two?

He despises and treats with contempt those beginner bodhisattvas who have not long practiced; he does not cause them to grasp [the teachings], nor does he analyze or instruct them. And because of that very same deep-seated conviction, he becomes disrespectful toward the training;
he favors sentient beings only by giving worldly material goods.

Not by the gift of Dharma. Maitreya, it is through these two causes that a bodhisattva who is resolved upon the profound exhausts himself and does not quickly attain the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena.
When this had been said, the bodhisattva Maitreya addressed the Blessed One as follows: "It is wonderful, Blessed One, how well-spoken is the word of the Blessed One!
Blessed One, we shall avoid these faults."
We shall protect and uphold this unexcelled, perfect enlightenment of the Tathāgata, which was achieved through hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of incalculable eons.
Furthermore, we shall place these very sūtras into the hands of those sons and daughters of good family in the future who have become worthy vessels;
and we shall bestow upon them such mindfulness that, by means of that mindfulness, they will take delight in and master these very sūtras.
They will master, uphold, propagate, write down, and explain in detail to others these [teachings].
And, O Blessed One, we shall provide support for them—
those indeed who, at that time, O Blessed One, shall take delight in and propagate such sūtras as these.
"Blessed One, it should be understood that this is the empowerment of the bodhisattva Maitreya.
Then the Blessed One gave his approval to the bodhisattva Maitreya: "Excellent, excellent, Maitreya!"
"This speech of yours is well-spoken; the Tathāgata rejoices in it and approves of what has been well-spoken. Then those bodhisattvas spoke these words in a single voice:
“Blessed One, after the Tathāgata has entered final nirvāṇa, we too shall come from our respective buddha-fields and cause this awakening of the Tathāgata’s buddhahood to spread widely;
and we shall announce it to those sons of good family.
Then the four great kings said this to the Blessed One:

"O Blessed One, wherever in villages, towns, market-towns, kingdoms, or royal capitals these such discourses on the Dharma shall circulate, be taught, and be proclaimed, there, O Blessed One, we four Great Kings, together with our armies, our mounts, and our retinues, will approach to hear the Dharma. And for that preacher of the Dharma, we will provide protection for a hundred leagues all around."
"so that no one seeking an opportunity, searching for an opening, shall find an opportunity against that Dharma-preacher.
Then the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda:
"Ānanda, take up this Dharma-discourse; retain it, recite it, and reveal it extensively to others."
He said: "I have grasped this Dharma-discourse, Blessed One. What, Blessed One, is the name of this Dharma-discourse? And how should I remember it?"
The Blessed One said:

"Therefore, Ānanda, you should remember this Dharma discourse as 'The Teaching of Vimalakīrti,' or as 'The Array of Pairs and Reversals,' or even as 'The Chapter on the Liberation of the Inconceivable Dharma.'"
The Blessed One spoke thus.

The Licchavi Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī the Youthful, the Venerable Ānanda, those great śrāvakas, and the entire assembly— including the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas— were uplifted in spirit by the Blessed One’s words.
They rejoiced in what was spoken.
The twelfth chapter, titled "The Conclusion and Entrustment."
Of those phenomena that arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.

This is the religious gift of the monk Śīladhvaja, a follower of the most excellent Mahāyāna; whatever merit is herein, may it, placing his preceptors, teachers, mother, and father at the forefront, be for the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge by the entire multitude of sentient beings.
This was written on the 29th day of Bhādra in the year 12 during the reign of the illustrious King Gopāla by the attendant Cāṇḍoka.
